option_analysis.diagnosis: Medieval South Indian garments had terms like veshti, pudavai, or uttariya, not fanam.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Material culture distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Fanam is numismatic, not sartorial.

option_analysis.label: Coins
option_analysis.diagnosis: Fanam was a famous historical South Indian currency denomination (gold and silver coin).
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Numismatic terminology testing rooted in medieval South Indian economic history.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Fanam = Panam = Coins.

option_analysis.label: Ornaments
option_analysis.diagnosis: Ornaments were known by terms such as kundala, valayal, or haras.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Plausible luxury item distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Fanam was legal tender/money, not jewellery.

option_analysis.label: Weapons
option_analysis.diagnosis: Medieval weaponry terms included katar, churika, khadga, not fanam.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Military hardware distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Fanam is not a weapon.

subject: History & Culture
sub_topic: Freedom Struggle - Revolutionary Movements & Ghadar Party
question_text:
Consider the following freedom fighters:
1. Barindra Kumar Ghosh
2. Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee
3. Rash Behari Bose
Who of the above was/were actively associated with the Ghadar Party?
explanation:
1. Barindra Kumar Ghosh was a core leader of the revolutionary Jugantar group in Bengal and was arrested in the 1908 Alipore Bomb Conspiracy case and sentenced to transportation for life to the Cellular Jail in the Andamans. He was not associated with the Ghadar Party.
2. Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee was a member of the Anushilan Samiti and later a co-founder of the Hindustan Republican Association (HRA) in 1924, arrested in the Kakori Conspiracy case (1925). He was not actively associated with the Ghadar Party.
3. Rash Behari Bose was the master planner who orchestrated the 1912 bomb attack on Viceroy Lord Hardinge. When World War I broke out, he was chosen by the Ghadar leadership in North America to lead the planned pan-India armed insurrection (the Ghadar Mutiny of February 1915). Following its betrayal, he escaped to Japan, where he continued his revolutionary struggle, eventually founding the Indian Independence League and laying the groundwork for the Indian National Army (INA).
Thus, only Rash Behari Bose (3 only) was actively associated with the Ghadar Party.
standard_book_ref: A Brief History of Modern India by Spectrum (Rajiv Ahir), Chapter 14: First Phase of Revolutionary Activities; Bipan Chandra - India's Struggle for Independence, Chapter 12.
elimination_trap: Barindra Ghosh was imprisoned in the Andamans when the Ghadar Party was formed (1913). Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee was an HRA leader in the 1920s. Rash Behari Bose was the undisputed link coordinating the North American Ghadarites with revolutionary soldiers in Punjab and Bengal in 1915.

mains_linkage.question: Assess the contribution of overseas revolutionary networks, particularly the Ghadar Party and the Indian Independence League, to India's freedom struggle.

option_analysis.label: 1 and 2
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits Rash Behari Bose while grouping two revolutionary leaders who belonged to Jugantar and HRA respectively.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Groups revolutionary figures across disparate chronological phases.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Barindra Ghosh was in Cellular Jail; Jogesh Chatterjee was in HRA/Kakori.

option_analysis.label: 2 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee was an HRA leader, not a Ghadarite.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Tests specific organizational affiliations within the revolutionary movement.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Chatterjee = HRA (Kakori), not Ghadar.

option_analysis.label: 1 and 3
option_analysis.diagnosis: Pairs Barindra Ghosh with Rash Behari Bose; Barindra was serving a life sentence in Port Blair during the Ghadar uprising.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Tempts candidates who know both were prominent early Bengal revolutionaries.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Barindra had no involvement with Ghadar Party.

option_analysis.label: 3 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Rash Behari Bose was the supreme coordinator of the 1915 Ghadar armed rebellion in India.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Pinpoints the historical convergence between domestic and expatriate revolutionary plots during WWI.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Only Rash Behari Bose led the Ghadar conspiracy in India.

subject: History & Culture
sub_topic: Freedom Struggle - Cripps Mission Proposals (1942)
question_text:
With reference to the proposals of Cripps Mission, consider the following statements:
1. The Constituent Assembly would have members nominated by the Provincial Assemblies as well as the Princely States.
2. Any Province, which is not prepared to accept the new Constitution would have the right to sign a separate agreement with Britain regarding its future status.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation:
In March 1942, Sir Stafford Cripps brought the British War Cabinet's proposals to India:
1. Regarding the Constituent Assembly: The proposals stipulated that the constitution-making body would consist of members ELECTED by the lower houses of the Provincial Assemblies (via proportional representation) and members NOMINATED by the rulers of the Princely States. Statement 1 falsely asserts that members from Provincial Assemblies would be 'nominated'. Therefore, statement 1 is incorrect.
2. Regarding provincial secession: The Cripps proposals explicitly stated that any province that was not prepared to accept the new Constitution would have the right to retain its existing constitutional position or frame a constitution of its own and enter into a separate direct treaty/agreement with the British Government, giving identical status to that of the Indian Union. This 'local option' clause contained the blueprint for India's partition. Statement 2 is correct.
standard_book_ref: A Brief History of Modern India by Spectrum (Rajiv Ahir), Chapter 22: Nationalist Upsurge at the End of World War II; Bipan Chandra - India's Struggle for Independence, Chapter 35.
elimination_trap: Carefully read the phrasing in statement 1: 'nominated by the Provincial Assemblies'. Provincial representatives were to be elected, while only Princely State representatives were to be nominated. This precise wordplay makes statement 1 incorrect.

mains_linkage.question: Examine why the Cripps Mission of 1942 failed to satisfy either the Indian National Congress or the Muslim League, and discuss how its 'provincial option' clause paved the way for Partition.

option_analysis.label: 1 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Provincial Assembly members were to be elected through proportional representation, not nominated.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Classic UPSC trap replacing 'elected' with 'nominated' in constitutional schemes.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Provincial assemblies elected their members; only princely states nominated them.

option_analysis.label: 2 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Statement 2 is historically accurate: the Cripps offer explicitly gave non-acceding provinces the right to form separate dominions with Britain.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Tests deep textual familiarity with the controversial 'local option' clause of the Cripps Declaration.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Cripps allowed provinces to secede and sign separate treaties with Britain (true).

option_analysis.label: Both 1 and 2
option_analysis.diagnosis: Accepts statement 1 without noticing the 'nominated' distortion.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Lures candidates who recall the presence of both provinces and princely states but miss the mode of selection.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Provinces = elected, not nominated.

option_analysis.label: Neither 1 nor 2
option_analysis.diagnosis: Rejects statement 2, ignoring the very clause that Congress condemned as an invitation to balkanize India.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Underestimates the divisive terms of the 1942 declaration.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Statement 2 was the primary point of contention for Congress.

subject: History & Culture
sub_topic: Ancient & Medieval Literature - Jaina Texts
question_text:
With reference to Indian history, consider the following texts:
1. Nettipakarana
2. Parishishtaparvan
3. Avadanashataka
4. Trishashtilakshana Mahapurana
Which of the above are Jaina texts?
explanation:
1. Nettipakarana ('The Book of Guidance') is a canonical/paracanonical Buddhist scripture in the Pali language, traditionally attributed to Mahakaccana and included in the Khuddaka Nikaya of the Sutta Pitaka. It is a Buddhist text.
2. Parishishtaparvan ('The Appendix'), also titled Sthaviravalicharitra, was written in Sanskrit by the great 12th-century Jaina polymath Acharya Hemachandra. It provides a detailed hagiography of ancient Jain elders and monarchs like Chandragupta Maurya. It is a Jaina text.
3. Avadanashataka ('A Hundred Stories of Virtuous Deeds') is a famous 2nd-century CE Sanskrit Buddhist anthology belonging to the Sarvastivada / Mulasarvastivada tradition containing stories of the Buddha and Bodhisattvas. It is a Buddhist text.
4. Trishashtilakshana Mahapurana (or simply Mahapurana) is a monumental 9th-century Digambara Jaina Sanskrit epic composed by Acharya Jinasena and completed by his disciple Gunabhadra. It narrates the lives of the 63 illustrious persons (Trishashtishalaka Purushas) of Jainism. It is a Jaina text.
Therefore, only 2 and 4 are Jaina texts.
standard_book_ref: A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India by Upinder Singh, Chapter 6: Cities, Kings, and Renunciants; NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I.
elimination_trap: Nettipakarana and Avadanashataka are well-known Buddhist texts ('Avadana' literature is exclusively Buddhist, e.g. Divyavadana, Ashokavadana). Recognizing Avadanashataka as Buddhist immediately eliminates 3, which knocks out options (a), (c), and (d) all at once, leaving (b) 2 and 4 only.

mains_linkage.question: Examine the contributions of Jaina and Buddhist canonical and biographical literature to the reconstruction of social and political history of ancient India.

option_analysis.label: 1, 2 and 3
option_analysis.diagnosis: Includes Nettipakarana (Pali Buddhist) and Avadanashataka (Sanskrit Buddhist).
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Mixes major Buddhist textual traditions with Jain works.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Avadana is Buddhist; eliminate 3.

option_analysis.label: 2 and 4 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Parishishtaparvan (by Hemachandra) and Mahapurana (by Jinasena and Gunabhadra) are celebrated Jain classics.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Tests deep religious literature classification across Buddhist and Jain corpora.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Parishishtaparvan = Jain, Mahapurana = Jain; Nettipakarana = Pali Buddhist, Avadanashataka = Buddhist -> 2 and 4 only.

option_analysis.label: 1, 3 and 4
option_analysis.diagnosis: Includes Buddhist texts 1 and 3 while dropping Hemachandra's Parishishtaparvan.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Omits the most famous Jain historical chronicle.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Parishishtaparvan must be present.

option_analysis.label: 2, 3 and 4
option_analysis.diagnosis: Retains Buddhist Avadanashataka alongside the two Jain epics.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Catches candidates unaware that Avadana signifies Buddhist narrative tales.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Avadana is Buddhist, not Jain.

subject: History & Culture
sub_topic: Ancient & Medieval Philosophical Traditions - Scholars
question_text:
Consider the following pairs:
Historical person — Known as
1. Aryadeva — Jaina scholar
2. Dignaga — Buddhist scholar
3. Nathamuni — Vaishnava scholar
How many pairs given above are correctly matched?
explanation:
1. Aryadeva (3rd century CE) was a renowned Mahayana Buddhist philosopher and the foremost disciple of Nagarjuna. He authored the fundamental Madhyamaka treatise 'Chatuhshataka' (Four Hundred Stanzas). He was a Buddhist scholar, NOT a Jaina scholar. Pair 1 is incorrectly matched.
2. Dignaga (c. 480–540 CE) was a seminal Buddhist scholar and the founder of Buddhist epistemology (Pramana) and Indian formal Buddhist logic. He authored the 'Pramana-samucchaya'. Pair 2 is correctly matched.
3. Nathamuni (9th-10th century CE) was a legendary Vaishnava theologian and the first of the great acharyas of Sri Vaishnavism. He collected and codified the 4,000 Tamil devotional hymns of the Alvars known as the 'Nalayira Divya Prabandham' and composed the Sanskrit works Nyayatattva and Yogarahasya. Pair 3 is correctly matched.
Therefore, only two pairs (2 and 3) are correctly matched.
standard_book_ref: A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India by Upinder Singh, Chapter 7 & 9; AL Basham - The Wonder That Was India; NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II.
elimination_trap: Aryadeva is paired with Jainism to mislead candidates unfamiliar with Nagarjuna's lineage. Recognizing Aryadeva as the author of the Madhyamaka text Chatuhshataka immediately clarifies that only Dignaga (Buddhist) and Nathamuni (Vaishnava) are correct.

mains_linkage.question: Trace the evolution of early medieval Bhakti philosophical theology with special reference to the contribution of Sri Vaishnava Acharyas in South India.

option_analysis.label: None of the pairs
option_analysis.diagnosis: Falsely rejects all pairs despite Dignaga and Nathamuni being globally renowned figures in their respective traditions.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Extreme negative choice.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Dignaga and Nathamuni are definitely correct.

option_analysis.label: Only one pair
option_analysis.diagnosis: Under-counts the valid pairs, missing either Dignaga or Nathamuni.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Partial identification.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Both Dignaga (Buddhist logic) and Nathamuni (Vaishnava Prabandham) are matched correctly.

option_analysis.label: Only two pairs
option_analysis.diagnosis: Pairs 2 and 3 are correctly matched. Aryadeva was a Madhyamaka Buddhist, not a Jaina scholar.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Pair-counting structure testing philosophical religious identities across ancient/medieval eras.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Aryadeva = Buddhist (not Jain); Dignaga = Buddhist; Nathamuni = Vaishnava -> exactly two pairs.

option_analysis.label: All three pairs
option_analysis.diagnosis: Accepts Aryadeva as a Jain scholar, missing his famous association as Nagarjuna's premier student.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Lures candidates assuming all pairs are valid.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Aryadeva was Buddhist.

subject: History & Culture
sub_topic: Delhi Sultanate - Mongol Invasions
question_text:
With reference to Indian history, consider the following statements:
1. The first Mongol invasion of India happened during the reign of Jalal-ud-din Khalji.
2. During the reign of Ala-ud-din Khalji, one Mongol assault marched up to Delhi and besieged the city.
3. Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq temporarily lost portions of north-west of his kingdom to Mongols.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation:
1. The first Mongol invasion of the Indian subcontinent occurred much earlier, in 1221 CE, during the reign of Shamsuddin Iltutmish of the Slave (Mamluk) Dynasty, when Genghis Khan pursued the fugitive Shah of Khwarizm, Jalal-ud-din Mangbarani, up to the banks of the Indus. Later Mongol incursions occurred during the reigns of Balban. Statement 1 is incorrect.
2. In 1303 CE, during the reign of Ala-ud-din Khalji, a formidable Mongol army under Taraghai marched with astonishing speed directly to Delhi, caught Alauddin unprepared while his forces were away besieging Chittor, and laid siege to Delhi for months. Alauddin was forced to take refuge in the Siri fortress. Statement 2 is correct.
3. During the reign of Muhammad bin Tughlaq, the Chagatai Mongol leader Tarmashirin invaded India (c. 1326-1327 CE) and advanced towards Delhi, but Muhammad bin Tughlaq defeated the Mongols and repulsed them back beyond the Indus, even planning an expedition to Khurasan to secure his northwestern frontiers. Muhammad bin Tughlaq did NOT lose portions of the north-west to the Mongols. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Therefore, statement 2 only is correct.
standard_book_ref: NCERT Class 11 - Medieval India by Satish Chandra, Chapter 6: The Delhi Sultanat - II (The Khaljis and the Tughlaqs); Advanced Study in the History of Medieval India by J.L. Mehta.
elimination_trap: Statement 1 is an elementary factual error: Genghis Khan came to the Indus during Iltutmish's rule (1221). Eliminating statement 1 immediately knocks out (a) and (c). Between (b) 2 only and (d) 3 only, Taraghai's famous siege of Delhi in 1303 is an iconic historical event that compelled Alauddin to build Siri and introduce his celebrated market reforms.

mains_linkage.question: Examine the impact of the recurring Mongol invasions on the administrative, military, and economic policies of the Delhi Sultanate under the Khaljis and Tughlaqs.

option_analysis.label: 1 and 2
option_analysis.diagnosis: Includes statement 1. Mongol incursions started in 1221 under Iltutmish, decades before Jalaluddin Khalji.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Distorts Sultanate timeline.
option_analysis.mental_filter: First Mongol arrival was under Iltutmish (Genghis Khan).

option_analysis.label: 2 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Only statement 2 is correct: the Mongol commander Taraghai surrounded and besieged Delhi in 1303, forcing Alauddin Khalji into Siri.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Highlights one of the most critical military crises in the history of the Delhi Sultanate.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Taraghai besieged Delhi under Alauddin (true); Mongols did not take NW territory from MBT.

option_analysis.label: 1 and 3
option_analysis.diagnosis: Pairs both false historical claims while dropping the famous siege of Siri.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Inverted selection.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Statements 1 and 3 are historically incorrect.

option_analysis.label: 3 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Muhammad bin Tughlaq pushed the Mongols beyond the Indus and never ceded northwestern territory to them.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Plays on MBT's reputation for administrative blunders to assume he lost territory.
option_analysis.mental_filter: MBT defeated Tarmashirin's Mongol raid.

subject: History & Culture
sub_topic: Medieval Social Groups - Kulah-Daran
question_text: With reference to Indian history, who of the following were known as "Kulah-Daran"?
explanation: In medieval India under the Delhi Sultanate, the Sayyids (the elite Muslim community claiming direct lineal descent from the Prophet Muhammad through his daughter Fatima) commanded immense social prestige and religious deference. The Sayyids were customarily distinguished by their distinctive headgear—a tall, conical pointed cap known in Persian as a 'kulah'. Consequently, the Sayyids were popularly designated in court chronicles and contemporary historical literature as 'Kulah-Daran' (literally 'cap-wearers').
standard_book_ref: NCERT Class 11 - Medieval India by Satish Chandra; A History of the Delhi Sultanate by K.S. Lal; Comprehensive History of India (Vol 5).
elimination_trap: Candidates often guess Qalandars (wandering Sufi dervishes) because of their unorthodox ascetic attire. However, 'Kulah-Daran' specifically denoted the high-status Sayyids wearing the ceremonial pointed cap.

mains_linkage.question: Examine the social stratification and the status of religious elites (Ulema, Sayyids, and Sufis) during the Delhi Sultanate.

option_analysis.label: Arab merchants
option_analysis.diagnosis: Arab merchants traded along the Malabar and Coromandel coasts and were called Hanjamana or Pardesi, not Kulah-Daran.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Commercial mercantile group distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Arab merchants had maritime designations, not Kulah-Daran.

option_analysis.label: Qalandars
option_analysis.diagnosis: Qalandars were antinomian, wandering, ecstatic Sufi dervishes known for shaven heads and begging bowls.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Appeals to candidates looking for an eccentric religious sect.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Qalandars were mendicant dervishes, not the dignified Kulah-Daran.

option_analysis.label: Persian calligraphists
option_analysis.diagnosis: Calligraphists were known as Khush-navis or Katib.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Artistic profession distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Calligraphists were Katibs/Khushnavis.

option_analysis.label: Sayyids
option_analysis.diagnosis: The Sayyids of the Delhi Sultanate claimed descent from the Prophet and wore distinctive pointed caps (kulah), earning them the title Kulah-Daran.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Testing socio-cultural terminology of medieval elite classes.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Kulah-Daran = pointed cap wearers = Sayyids.

subject: History & Culture
sub_topic: Colonial Expansion - European Settlements in India
question_text:
With reference to Indian history, consider the following statements:
1. The Dutch established their factories/warehouses on the east coast on lands granted to them by Gajapati rulers.
2. Alfonso de Albuquerque captured Goa from the Bijapur Sultanate.
3. The English East India Company established a factory at Madras on a plot of land leased from a representative of the Vijayanagara Empire.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation:
1. The Gajapati dynasty of Odisha collapsed in the mid-16th century (Mukunda Deva died in 1568 and Odisha fell to the Afghans/Mughals). The Dutch East India Company (VOC) was established in 1602 and founded factories on the east coast (such as Pulicat, Masulipatnam, and later Nizampatnam/Bimlipatam) in the 17th century on grants from the Golconda Sultanate and local Nayakas, long after the Gajapati dynasty had ceased to exist. Statement 1 is incorrect.
2. In 1510, the Portuguese governor Alfonso de Albuquerque captured the strategic port of Goa from Ismail Adil Shah, the Sultan of Bijapur, with the local assistance of Timoja. Statement 2 is correct.
3. In 1639, Francis Day of the English East India Company negotiated the grant of a strip of coastal land at Madraspatnam from Damarla Venkatadri Nayaka, the Nayaka of Vandavasi, who was a local chieftain and feudatory representative of Peda Venkata Raya (Venkata III) of the Aravidu dynasty of the Vijayanagara Empire (ruling from Chandragiri). Fort St. George was erected on this leased land. Statement 3 is correct.
Therefore, statements 2 and 3 only are correct.
standard_book_ref: A Brief History of Modern India by Spectrum (Rajiv Ahir), Chapter 3: Advent of the Europeans in India; NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part III; Bipan Chandra - Modern India.
elimination_trap: Chronological awareness easily eliminates statement 1: Gajapati rulers ruled Odisha in the 15th and early 16th centuries, while Dutch trading presence commenced in the 1600s. Eliminating 1 knocks out (a), (c), and (d), leaving (b) 2 and 3 only.

mains_linkage.question: Examine the political fragmentation of peninsular India in the 16th and 17th centuries and how it aided early European commercial and territorial footholds.

option_analysis.label: 1 and 2 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Includes statement 1. The Dutch arrived decades after the fall of the Gajapatis.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Anachronistic juxtaposition of medieval Indian dynasties with European colonial companies.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Gajapatis ended in 1568; Dutch VOC arrived in the 1600s; 1 is false.

option_analysis.label: 2 and 3 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Statements 2 and 3 are correct: Albuquerque captured Goa from Bijapur in 1510, and Madras was leased in 1639 from Nayakas subordinate to the Vijayanagara ruler at Chandragiri.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Standard colonial history question testing landmark territorial acquisitions.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Albuquerque took Goa from Bijapur (1510); Madras leased from Vijayanagara Nayaka (1639) = 2 and 3.

option_analysis.label: 1 and 3 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits statement 2, which is the foundational event of Portuguese rule in India.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Drops the iconic 1510 Portuguese conquest of Goa.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Albuquerque capturing Goa is a cardinal fact.

option_analysis.label: 1, 2 and 3
option_analysis.diagnosis: Accepts anachronistic statement 1.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: All-inclusive trap for candidates ignoring chronological gaps.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Statement 1 is chronologically impossible.

subject: History & Culture
sub_topic: Ancient Polity & Society - Kautilya's Arthashastra on Slavery
question_text:
According to Kautilya’s Arthashastra, which of the following are correct?
1. A person could be a slave as a result of a judicial punishment.
2. If a female slave bore her master a son, she was legally free.
3. If a son born to a female slave was fathered by her master, the son was entitled to the legal status of the master's son.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation:
Kautilya's Arthashastra (Book III, Chapter 13: 'Rules Regarding Slaves and Laborers' / Dasa-kalpa) provides an elaborate, humane legal framework governing slavery in the Mauryan period:
1. A person could be condemned to servitude (dasa) as a result of a judicial decree or penal punishment (danda-pranita), e.g. for failure to pay fines or judicial convictions. Statement 1 is correct.
2. Arthashastra explicitly lays down: 'When a child is begotten on a female slave by her master, both the child and its mother shall at once be recognized as free' (dasi-putra-matuh muktih). Thus, she was legally emancipated upon bearing a child to her master. Statement 2 is correct.
3. Furthermore, Arthashastra decrees that such a child fathered by the master on a slave woman had legal inheritance rights and was legally recognized as the legitimate son of the master, entitled to a share in property. Statement 3 is correct.
Hence, all 1, 2, and 3 are correct.
standard_book_ref: Kautilya's Arthashastra translated by R. Shamasastry (Book III, Chapter XIII); A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India by Upinder Singh, Chapter 6; NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I.
elimination_trap: Many candidates assumed that ancient slavery was as brutal and absolute as Greco-Roman chattel slavery (where slave children remained permanent chattels). Kautilya's Arthashastra provided unique progressive legal safeguards protecting Dasas from perpetual exploitation. All three statements are directly sourced from the Dasa-kalpa chapter.

mains_linkage.question: Compare the institution of slavery as depicted in Kautilya's Arthashastra with Megasthenes' observation that 'all Indians are free and not one of them is a slave'.

option_analysis.label: 1 and 2 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits statement 3. Kautilya granted legal status and paternity inheritance rights to the son born of the master.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Preys on Western conceptions of slavery where slave offspring had zero legal paternal rights.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Arthashastra recognized the son's legitimate legal status.

option_analysis.label: 2 and 3 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits statement 1. Judicial penal enslavement (dandapranita) is one of the classic categories of dasas in Arthashastra.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Excludes the state punitive origin of slavery.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Judicial punishment could lead to temporary/penal servitude in ancient India.

option_analysis.label: 1 and 3 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits statement 2. Emancipation of the mother upon childbirth was a celebrated humanitarian rule in Arthashastra.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Separates the mother's emancipation from the son's legal recognition.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Both mother and child gained freedom.

option_analysis.label: 1, 2 and 3
option_analysis.diagnosis: All three statements accurately reproduce Kautilya's legal stipulations in Book III, Chapter 13 of the Arthashastra.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Deep textual testing of ancient Indian jurisprudence and social institutions.
option_analysis.mental_filter: All three rules are explicitly recorded in Kautilya's Dasa-kalpa chapter.

subject: Economy
sub_topic: External Sector - Monetary Policy & Capital Flows
question_text:
Consider the following statements:
1. Tight monetary policy of US Federal Reserve could lead to capital flight.
2. Capital flight may increase the cost of firms with existing External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs).
3. Devaluation of domestic currency decreases the currency risk associated with ECBs.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation:
[NOTE: This question was officially DROPPED by UPSC in the Final Answer Key for Series A, marked with symbol 'X'. Evaluation for GS Paper-1 was conducted out of 99 questions].

Conceptual Analysis of Statements:
1. Tight monetary policy of US Federal Reserve raises US interest rates and yields on US Treasury securities, increasing the yield differential between US and emerging market assets. This triggers capital flight (outflow of foreign portfolio investment) from emerging markets like India back to dollar assets. (Statement 1 is conceptually correct).
2. Capital flight triggers depreciation of the domestic currency (Rupee) against the US dollar. For Indian firms with unhedged existing External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs) denominated in dollars, a weaker rupee requires more domestic currency to service dollar-denominated interest and principal repayments, substantially escalating debt servicing costs. (Statement 2 is conceptually correct).
3. Devaluation/depreciation of the domestic currency increases (rather than decreases) the currency risk associated with foreign currency-denominated ECBs, because borrowers must convert more local currency to purchase dollars. (Statement 3 is conceptually incorrect).

Why UPSC Dropped the Question:
UPSC dropped this question due to technical ambiguities in statement 2 and statement 3 concerning the precise definition of 'cost' for fixed-rate vs floating-rate existing ECBs, and the distinction between market-driven currency depreciation versus official currency devaluation under fixed/managed exchange rate regimes.
standard_book_ref: Indian Economy by Ramesh Singh - External Sector; NCERT Class 12 Macroeconomics - Open Economy Macroeconomics; RBI Bulletin on External Commercial Borrowings.
elimination_trap: This question was officially cancelled/dropped by UPSC. In the CookedMains PYQ vault, it is preserved with correct_option: 'X (Dropped by UPSC)' and correct_index: -1 to strictly adhere to the official final key.

option_analysis.examiner_craft: Intended answer, but invalidated post-exam by UPSC expert scrutiny.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Officially Dropped ('X') in the Master UPSC 2022 Key.

option_analysis.label: 2 and 3 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Question cancelled by UPSC.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Question dropped by UPSC.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Dropped by UPSC.

option_analysis.label: 1 and 3 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Question cancelled by UPSC.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Question dropped by UPSC.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Dropped by UPSC.

option_analysis.label: 1, 2 and 3
option_analysis.diagnosis: Question cancelled by UPSC.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Question dropped by UPSC.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Dropped by UPSC.

subject: Geography
sub_topic: Agricultural Geography - Tea-Producing States
question_text:
Consider the following States:
1. Andhra Pradesh
2. Kerala
3. Himachal Pradesh
4. Tripura
How many of the above are generally known as tea-producing States?
explanation:
According to the Tea Board of India and the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, tea is commercially cultivated across several states categorized into traditional and non-traditional tea-growing regions:
1. Andhra Pradesh: Cultivates tea in the high-altitude tribal agency tracts of Visakhapatnam district (notably Chintapalli, Paderu, and Araku Valley), recognized by the Tea Board as a non-traditional tea-producing area.
2. Kerala: A major traditional southern tea producer, with famous plantations across Wayanad, Idukki (Munnar), Thrissur, and Palakkad districts.
3. Himachal Pradesh: World-famous for GI-tagged Kangra Tea grown across the Kangra Valley, Palampur, and Mandi districts.
4. Tripura: The fifth-largest tea-producing state in India, with more than 50 operational tea gardens spread across Manu Valley, Sadar, and Kailashahar.
Therefore, all four States are recognized as tea-producing States in India.
standard_book_ref: Tea Board of India Official State Profiles; NCERT Class 10/12 Geography - Contemporary India (Agriculture); Ministry of Commerce and Industry Annual Reports.
elimination_trap: Many candidates doubted Andhra Pradesh or Tripura, assuming tea is confined only to Assam, West Bengal, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu. However, Kangra tea (HP) is famous, Tripura is India's 5th largest producer, and Araku Valley in AP has established commercial tea cultivation promoted by ITDA and the Tea Board. Official UPSC Key is (d) All four States.

mains_linkage.question: Discuss the geographical requirements for tea cultivation in India and examine the structural challenges faced by traditional and small tea growers.

option_analysis.label: Only one State
option_analysis.diagnosis: Grossly underestimates tea production, ignoring major producers like Kerala and Tripura.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Designed for candidates with minimal knowledge of Indian plantation agriculture.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Kerala, HP, and Tripura are unquestionably tea producers.

option_analysis.label: Only two States
option_analysis.diagnosis: Recognizes only Kerala and Himachal Pradesh, omitting Tripura (5th largest tea producer).
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Overlooks the Northeast outside Assam.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Tripura has over 50 commercial tea estates.

option_analysis.label: Only three States
option_analysis.diagnosis: Leaves out Andhra Pradesh, unaware of the high-altitude tea plantations in Araku and Paderu.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Tempting choice for candidates who know Kerala, HP, and Tripura but doubt AP.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Tea Board recognizes AP agency tracts as a tea-producing zone.

option_analysis.label: All four States
option_analysis.diagnosis: All four states (Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Himachal Pradesh, Tripura) commercially grow tea and are officially listed by the Tea Board of India.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Rewards exhaustive knowledge of state-level commercial crop cultivation profiles.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Kerala + HP + Tripura + AP = all four States.

subject: Economy
sub_topic: Financial Markets - Credit Rating Agencies
question_text:
Consider the following statements:
1. In India, credit rating agencies are regulated by Reserve Bank of India.
2. The rating agency popularly known as ICRA is a public limited company.
3. Brickwork Ratings is an Indian credit rating agency.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation:
1. In India, Credit Rating Agencies (CRAs) are regulated by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) under the SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999 (enacted under Section 30 of the SEBI Act, 1992), NOT by the Reserve Bank of India. Statement 1 is incorrect.
2. ICRA Limited (formerly Investment Information and Credit Rating Agency of India Limited) was set up in 1991 and is an independent, public limited company listed on both the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) and the National Stock Exchange (NSE). Statement 2 is correct.
3. Brickwork Ratings (BWR) is an Indian credit rating agency registered with SEBI and accredited by the RBI, offering ratings for bank loans, bonds, and municipal corporations. Statement 3 is correct.
Therefore, statements 2 and 3 only are correct.
standard_book_ref: Indian Economy by Ramesh Singh, Chapter: Financial Markets; SEBI Credit Rating Agencies Regulations, 1999; Indian Economy by Sanjiv Verma.
elimination_trap: Statement 1 is the primary elimination fulcrum: CRAs evaluate corporate debt securities, commercial papers, and bonds in capital markets, making SEBI their designated statutory regulator (not RBI). Eliminating 1 knocks out (a), (c), and (d) immediately.

mains_linkage.question: Analyze the systemic risks highlighted by the failure of credit rating agencies in forewarning corporate debt defaults (e.g., IL&FS) and evaluate regulatory reforms introduced by SEBI.

option_analysis.label: 1 and 2 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Includes statement 1. SEBI, not RBI, is the statutory regulator of Credit Rating Agencies in India.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Swaps regulatory jurisdictions between SEBI and RBI.
option_analysis.mental_filter: CRAs are regulated by SEBI, not RBI.

option_analysis.label: 2 and 3 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Statements 2 and 3 are correct: ICRA is a publicly listed company and Brickwork Ratings is a registered Indian CRA.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Tests awareness of regulatory oversight and major industry players in the Indian debt capital market.
option_analysis.mental_filter: SEBI regulates CRAs (1 is false); ICRA and Brickwork are Indian CRAs (2 and 3 are true).

option_analysis.label: 1 and 3 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Retains false statement 1 while omitting ICRA's corporate status.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Alternative pairing keeping the false RBI regulatory claim.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Statement 1 is incorrect.

option_analysis.label: 1, 2 and 3
option_analysis.diagnosis: Accepts statement 1, failing to recognize SEBI's exclusive oversight over CRAs.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: All-inclusive trap for candidates assuming the central bank controls credit rating.
option_analysis.mental_filter: RBI does not regulate CRAs; SEBI does.

subject: Economy
sub_topic: Banking Sector Reforms - Banks Board Bureau
question_text:
With reference to the "Banks Board Bureau (BBB)", which of the following statements are correct?
1. The Governor of RBI is the Chairman of BBB.
2. BBB recommends for the selection of heads for Public Sector Banks.
3. BBB helps the Public Sector Banks in developing strategies and capital raising plans.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
explanation:
1. The Banks Board Bureau (BBB, recommended by the P.J. Nayak Committee and constituted in 2016 under the Indradhanush framework) was headed by an independent Part-time Chairman appointed by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (the inaugural chairman was Vinod Rai, former CAG). The Governor of the RBI is NOT the Chairman of BBB (an RBI Deputy Governor was merely an ex-officio member). Statement 1 is incorrect.
2. BBB was specifically mandated to search, interview, and recommend competent professionals for appointment as whole-time directors and Non-Executive Chairmen of Public Sector Banks (PSBs) and public sector financial institutions. Statement 2 is correct.
3. BBB was also entrusted with advising the government on PSB board compositions, helping banks formulate growth strategies, and assisting in their capital raising and restructuring plans. Statement 3 is correct.
Therefore, statements 2 and 3 only are correct.
(Note: BBB has since been restructured and renamed as the Financial Services Institutions Bureau - FSIB in 2022).
standard_book_ref: Indian Economy by Ramesh Singh - Banking System in India; Economic Survey - Financial Intermediation; P.J. Nayak Committee Report on Governance of Boards of Banks in India.
elimination_trap: Vinod Rai (former CAG) was famously appointed as the first Chairman of BBB, making it clear that the RBI Governor does not chair it. Eliminating statement 1 instantly rules out (a), (c), and (d), leaving (b) 2 and 3 only.

mains_linkage.question: Examine the role of the Banks Board Bureau (now FSIB) in improving corporate governance, managerial autonomy, and human resource selection in Public Sector Banks.

option_analysis.label: 1 and 2 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Includes statement 1. The RBI Governor is not the head of the BBB; an independent eminent expert chairs it.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Plausible assumption that the central bank governor heads bank governance bodies.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Vinod Rai was first chairman, not the RBI Governor.

option_analysis.label: 2 and 3 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Statements 2 and 3 are correct: BBB selects PSB leadership and advises banks on strategy and capital raising.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Standard governance testing of the P.J. Nayak Committee banking reform architecture.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Chairman is independent (1 is false); recommends bank chiefs (true); helps strategy and capital (true) = 2 and 3 only.

option_analysis.label: 1 and 3 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits statement 2 (the core raison d'etre of the BBB) while keeping the false RBI Governor claim.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Inverted distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Recommending PSB heads was BBB's foremost visible mandate.

option_analysis.label: 1, 2 and 3
option_analysis.diagnosis: Accepts statement 1 without scrutiny.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: All-inclusive trap.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Statement 1 is false.

subject: Economy
sub_topic: Capital Markets - Convertible Bonds
question_text:
With reference to Convertible Bonds, consider the following statements:
1. As there is an option to exchange the bond for equity, Convertible Bonds pay a lower rate of interest.
2. The option to convert to equity affords the bondholder a degree of indexation to rising consumer prices.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation:
1. Convertible bonds are hybrid debt securities that grant the investor the embedded option to convert the debt into a predetermined number of equity shares of the issuing company. Because this equity conversion option holds financial value (allowing participation in company upside), issuers can offer a lower coupon (interest rate) than comparable non-convertible vanilla bonds. Statement 1 is correct.
2. Fixed-income bonds suffer real purchasing power erosion during inflation. However, equity shares generally appreciate alongside rising corporate revenues and consumer price inflation. Because convertible bonds allow conversion into equity shares, they provide investors with a built-in hedge or degree of indexation against inflation compared to pure fixed-income debt. Statement 2 is correct.
Therefore, both 1 and 2 are correct.
standard_book_ref: Principles of Corporate Finance by Brealey & Myers; Indian Economy by Ramesh Singh - Financial Markets; Investopedia & RBI Financial Instruments Guide.
elimination_trap: Candidates often doubted statement 2, wondering if 'indexation to rising consumer prices' meant formal government-indexed bonds (like IIBs). In corporate finance, conversion to equity is standardly described as providing an inflation hedge (indexation to rising prices/earnings). Both statements are fundamentally sound.

mains_linkage.question: Explain the role of hybrid financial instruments like convertible bonds and REITs in deepening India's corporate bond market and managing corporate capital structures.

option_analysis.label: 1 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits statement 2. Convertible bonds participate in equity growth, hedging the investor against consumer price inflation.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Tempts candidates who take a strict narrow definition of 'indexation'.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Equity upside offsets purchasing power loss, providing indexation.

option_analysis.label: 2 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits statement 1. The embedded conversion option universally allows issuers to pay lower coupon rates.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Disregards the basic cost-of-capital advantage of convertible bonds.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Convertible bonds pay lower interest than straight bonds.

option_analysis.label: Both 1 and 2
option_analysis.diagnosis: Both statements accurately reflect the corporate finance mechanics and investor risk-return dynamics of convertible bonds.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Rigorous financial instrument concept testing.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Lower coupon due to conversion option (true) + equity upside provides inflation indexation (true) = Both 1 and 2.

option_analysis.label: Neither 1 nor 2
option_analysis.diagnosis: Rejects both foundational financial principles.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Skeptical option.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Both statements are standard finance principles.

subject: Economy
sub_topic: International Organizations & Regimes - India's Membership
question_text:
Consider the following:
1. Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank
2. Missile Technology Control Regime
3. Shanghai Cooperation Organisation
India is a member of which of the above?
explanation:
1. Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB): India is a founding member (joined in 2016) and the second-largest shareholder (after China) with 7.6% voting share, and the largest recipient of project financing. (India is a member)
2. Missile Technology Control Regime (MTCR): India was admitted as the 35th full member of the MTCR on June 27, 2016, following its non-proliferation track record and international civil nuclear cooperation agreements. (India is a member)
3. Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO): India was admitted as a full member of the SCO at the Astana Summit in June 2017 (alongside Pakistan). (India is a member)
Therefore, India is a member of all three: 1, 2, and 3.
standard_book_ref: Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) Briefs on Multilateral Groupings; A Brief History of Modern India by Spectrum; NCERT Class 12 Political Science - Contemporary World Politics.
elimination_trap: Straightforward international relations question. India is not a member of the Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG), but it successfully joined MTCR, Wassenaar Arrangement, and Australia Group, and is a prominent full member of both AIIB and SCO.

mains_linkage.question: Analyze the strategic significance of India's entry into multilateral export control regimes like the MTCR, Wassenaar Arrangement, and Australia Group for its defense and space programs.

option_analysis.label: 1 and 2 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits SCO, of which India has been a full member since 2017.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Excludes a major Eurasian multilateral bloc.
option_analysis.mental_filter: India is a full member of SCO (Astana 2017).

option_analysis.label: 2 and 3 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits AIIB, despite India being its second-largest shareholder and top borrower.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Leaves out the Beijing-headquartered development bank.
option_analysis.mental_filter: India is a founding member and second-biggest stakeholder in AIIB.

option_analysis.label: 1 and 3 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits MTCR, confusing it with the NSG where India's membership has been blocked.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Capitalizes on confusion between MTCR (admitted 2016) and NSG (pending).
option_analysis.mental_filter: India joined MTCR in 2016.

option_analysis.label: 1, 2 and 3
option_analysis.diagnosis: India is a full member of AIIB, MTCR, and SCO.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Direct assessment of India's multilateral diplomatic accessions.
option_analysis.mental_filter: All three are memberships held by India.

subject: Economy
sub_topic: Global Economics - Vietnam Economic Model
question_text:
Consider the following statements:
1. Vietnam has been one of the fastest growing economies in the world in the recent years.
2. Vietnam is led by a multi-party political system.
3. Vietnam's economic growth is linked to its integration with global supply chains and focus on exports.
4. For a long time Vietnam's low labour costs and stable exchange rates have attracted foreign investment.
5. Vietnam has the most productive e-service sector in the Indo-Pacific region.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation:
1. Vietnam has emerged as one of the fastest-growing economies globally over the past two decades, consistently registering GDP growth rates of 6-7% and demonstrating remarkable resilience. Statement 1 is correct.
2. Vietnam is a single-party socialist republic governed exclusively by the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV). There is no multi-party political system. Statement 2 is incorrect.
3. Under its 'Doi Moi' economic reforms, Vietnam pursued an aggressive export-led growth strategy, entering numerous free trade agreements (CPTPP, EVFTA, RCEP) and becoming a major manufacturing node in global electronics and textile supply chains. Statement 3 is correct.
4. Competitive and low labor costs, demographic dividends, stable exchange rates, and favorable tax incentives have made Vietnam a prime destination for global foreign direct investment (e.g., massive manufacturing plants by Samsung, Foxconn, and Intel). Statement 4 is correct.
5. The claim that Vietnam has 'the most productive e-service sector in the Indo-Pacific region' is incorrect; countries like Singapore, Japan, South Korea, and Australia lead in e-service productivity by a wide margin. Statement 5 is incorrect.
Therefore, statements 1, 3, and 4 are correct.
standard_book_ref: World Bank Vietnam Development Reports; Economic Survey of India - Global Supply Chains; International Monetary Fund (IMF) Regional Economic Outlook.
elimination_trap: Statement 2 is an obvious political fact: Vietnam is a one-party communist state, making 'multi-party political system' blatantly false. Eliminating statement 2 immediately knocks out options (a) and (d). Between (b) and (c), statement 5 has an exaggerated superlative ('most productive e-service sector in the Indo-Pacific'), eliminating (b) and leaving (c) 1, 3 and 4.

mains_linkage.question: What lessons can India draw from Vietnam's export-oriented manufacturing success and supply chain integration under the 'China Plus One' global strategy?

option_analysis.label: 2 and 4
option_analysis.diagnosis: Includes statement 2. Vietnam is a single-party communist state, not a multi-party democracy.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Tests political geography fundamentals.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Vietnam is a one-party state; statement 2 is completely false.

option_analysis.label: 3 and 5
option_analysis.diagnosis: Includes statement 5. Singapore, South Korea, and Japan lead e-services, not Vietnam.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Pairs a correct economic trait with an unsubstantiated superlative.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Statement 5 is factually wrong.

option_analysis.label: 1, 3 and 4
option_analysis.diagnosis: Statements 1, 3, and 4 accurately describe Vietnam's rapid GDP expansion, export orientation, low labor costs, and FDI attraction.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Rewards understanding of East Asian manufacturing dynamics and China+1 supply chain shifts.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Rapid growth + export supply chains + low wages/stable FX = 1, 3 and 4.

option_analysis.label: 1 and 2
option_analysis.diagnosis: Retains false statement 2 regarding a multi-party system.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Pairs the true growth fact with the false political description.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Statement 2 is invalid.

subject: Economy
sub_topic: Monetary Policy - Inflation Targeting & Price Stability
question_text: In India, which one of the following is responsible for maintaining price stability by controlling inflation?
explanation: Under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 (as amended by the Finance Act, 2016), the primary statutory objective of monetary policy is explicitly defined: 'to maintain price stability while keeping in mind the objective of growth'. Under the Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) framework, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), through its six-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), is legally mandated and responsible for controlling Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation within the target band of 4% (+/- 2%).
standard_book_ref: Indian Economy by Ramesh Singh, Chapter: Monetary Policy; Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 (Preamble & Section 45ZA); Macroeconomics NCERT Class 12.
elimination_trap: While the Department of Consumer Affairs monitors retail prices of essential food commodities, statutory responsibility for controlling macroeconomic inflation and ensuring price stability is the sole legal mandate of the Reserve Bank of India.

mains_linkage.question: Examine the effectiveness of the Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) framework administered by the RBI in anchoring inflation expectations during supply-side global shocks.

option_analysis.label: Department of Consumer Affairs
option_analysis.diagnosis: Monitors essential commodity supplies and prices, but possesses no macroeconomic monetary policy mandate for inflation control.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Tempts candidates confusing retail essential commodity tracking with monetary price stability.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Statutory price stability mandate belongs to RBI.

option_analysis.label: Expenditure Management Commission
option_analysis.diagnosis: Advisory body (chaired formerly by Bimal Jalan) established to recommend public expenditure rationalization.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Fiscal committee distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Expenditure management is about government spending reforms.

option_analysis.label: Financial Stability and Development Council
option_analysis.diagnosis: Non-statutory apex body chaired by the Finance Minister dealing with macro-prudential regulation and inter-regulatory coordination.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Financial architecture distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: FSDC deals with financial sector stability and regulator coordination, not monetary inflation targeting.

option_analysis.label: Reserve Bank of India
option_analysis.diagnosis: The RBI has the exclusive statutory mandate under the RBI Act, 1934 to maintain price stability by controlling inflation through the Monetary Policy Committee.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Direct statutory mandate testing.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Maintaining price stability by controlling inflation = Reserve Bank of India (RBI).

subject: Science & Technology
sub_topic: Emerging Technologies - Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs)
question_text:
With reference to Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), consider the following statements:
1. They enable the digital representation of physical assets.
2. They are unique cryptographic tokens that exist on a blockchain.
3. They can be traded or exchanged at equivalency and therefore can be used as a medium of commercial transactions.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
explanation:
1. NFTs can represent real-world tangible assets (such as real estate deeds, physical artwork, or luxury goods) as well as purely digital files (digital art, music, collectibles) through tokenization, establishing verifiable ownership rights on-chain. Statement 1 is correct.
2. NFTs are unique cryptographic tokens that exist on a distributed ledger (blockchain) with distinct identification codes and metadata that distinguish them from any other token. Statement 2 is correct.
3. The defining characteristic of a 'non-fungible' asset is precisely that each unit is unique and CANNOT be exchanged or traded at equivalency. Fungible assets (like currency notes or Bitcoin) can be swapped at 1:1 equivalency, making them suitable as a standardized medium of commercial transactions. NFTs are non-fungible and cannot be exchanged at equivalency. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Therefore, statements 1 and 2 only are correct.
standard_book_ref: NITI Aayog National Strategy on Blockchain; World Economic Forum - Digital Assets Primer; IEEE Blockchain Guidelines.
elimination_trap: The name itself is 'NON-Fungible'. Statement 3 defines fungibility ('traded or exchanged at equivalency'). Since NFTs are non-fungible by definition, statement 3 is a direct contradiction of the core concept. Eliminating 3 leaves (a) 1 and 2 only.

mains_linkage.question: What are Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs)? Discuss their potential applications in intellectual property rights, digital art, and tokenization of real-world assets.

option_analysis.label: 1 and 2 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: NFTs tokenize physical/digital assets and exist as unique cryptographic tokens on a blockchain.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Elementary etymological testing: tests if candidates know what 'non-fungible' means.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Non-fungible = NOT interchangeable at equivalency; statement 3 is wrong, leaving 1 and 2.

option_analysis.label: 2 and 3 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Includes statement 3. Non-fungible tokens cannot be traded at equivalency like currency.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Tempts candidates who confuse cryptocurrency with NFTs.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Bitcoin is fungible; NFTs are non-fungible.

option_analysis.label: 1 and 3 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Retains false statement 3 while omitting the blockchain foundation in statement 2.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Inverted pairing.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Statement 3 contradicts the definition of NFT.

option_analysis.label: 1, 2 and 3
option_analysis.diagnosis: Accepts statement 3 without noticing the fundamental contradiction of 'fungibility'.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: All-inclusive trap.
option_analysis.mental_filter: NFT cannot be exchanged at equivalency.

subject: Geography
sub_topic: Water Resources - Dams & Reservoirs in India
question_text:
Consider the following pairs:
Reservoir — State
1. Ghataprabha — Telangana
2. Gandhi Sagar — Madhya Pradesh
3. Indira Sagar — Andhra Pradesh
4. Maithon — Chhattisgarh
How many pairs given above are not correctly matched?
explanation:
1. Ghataprabha Reservoir (Hidkal Dam) is situated across the Ghataprabha River in Belagavi district of Karnataka, not Telangana. Pair 1 is NOT correctly matched.
2. Gandhi Sagar Dam is located on the Chambal River in Mandsaur and Neemuch districts of Madhya Pradesh. Pair 2 is correctly matched.
3. Indira Sagar Dam is a massive multipurpose project located on the Narmada River in Khandwa district of Madhya Pradesh, not Andhra Pradesh (do not confuse with Indirasagar Polavaram in AP). Pair 3 is NOT correctly matched.
4. Maithon Dam is located on the Barakar River in Dhanbad district of Jharkhand (part of Damodar Valley Corporation), not Chhattisgarh. Pair 4 is NOT correctly matched.
Therefore, exactly three pairs (1, 3, and 4) are NOT correctly matched.
standard_book_ref: Central Water Commission (CWC) National Register of Large Dams; NCERT Class 10/12 Geography - Water Resources; Oxford Student Atlas for India.
elimination_trap: Notice the negative phrasing in the question: 'are NOT correctly matched'. Many candidates correctly recognized that Gandhi Sagar (MP) was the only correct pair, but in haste marked 'Only one pair' assuming the question asked for correctly matched pairs. The question asked how many are NOT correctly matched: exactly 3 pairs.

mains_linkage.question: Examine the spatial distribution of major multipurpose river valley projects in peninsular India and discuss their role in inter-state water disputes.

option_analysis.label: Only one pair
option_analysis.diagnosis: Only 1 pair is correctly matched, but the question asks how many are NOT correctly matched. Selecting this indicates a failure to read 'not'.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Classic inverted trap capitalizing on negative phrasing.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Read carefully: NOT correctly matched. Since 1 is correct, 3 are not correct.

option_analysis.label: Only two pairs
option_analysis.diagnosis: Assumes two pairs are mismatched instead of three.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Distractor for candidates uncertain about Ghataprabha or Maithon.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Ghataprabha (Karnataka), Indira Sagar (MP), Maithon (Jharkhand) = 3 wrong pairs.

option_analysis.label: Only three pairs
option_analysis.diagnosis: Pairs 1, 3, and 4 are mismatched (Ghataprabha is in Karnataka, Indira Sagar in MP, Maithon in Jharkhand). Exactly three pairs are not correctly matched.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Pair-counting with negative phrasing.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Ghataprabha!=Telangana (No), Gandhi Sagar==MP (Yes), Indira Sagar!=AP (No), Maithon!=Chhattisgarh (No) -> 3 not correctly matched.

option_analysis.label: All four pairs
option_analysis.diagnosis: Falsely assumes even Gandhi Sagar is mismatched.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Extreme option.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Gandhi Sagar on Chambal is in Madhya Pradesh.

subject: Economy
sub_topic: Labour & Employment - Statistical Organizations
question_text: In India, which one of the following compiles information on industrial disputes, closures, retrenchments and lay-offs in factories employing workers?
options: Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade
explanation: The Labour Bureau (an attached office under the Ministry of Labour and Employment, with offices at Chandigarh and Shimla) is the premier national agency entrusted with the collection, compilation, and dissemination of statistics on various facets of labor in India. Under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and the Collection of Statistics Act, the Labour Bureau collects and publishes monthly and annual statistics on industrial disputes (strikes and lockouts), closures, retrenchments, and lay-offs across registered factories and commercial establishments in India. It also compiles Consumer Price Index numbers for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW).
standard_book_ref: Ministry of Labour and Employment Annual Report; Indian Economy by Ramesh Singh; Indian Labour Statistics (Labour Bureau, Shimla).
elimination_trap: CSO (now NSO) compiles GDP and broad economic censuses, DPIIT promotes industrial investment and ease of doing business, but specialized labor statistical monitoring is the dedicated domain of the Labour Bureau.

mains_linkage.question: Examine the role of accurate labor market data in formulating social security and employment policies, and discuss the modernization initiatives undertaken by the Labour Bureau.

option_analysis.label: Central Statistics Office
option_analysis.diagnosis: CSO (merged into NSO under MoSPI) handles macroeconomic statistics like National Accounts and IIP, not specialized industrial dispute records.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Premier national statistical body distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: NSO/CSO does national accounts, not factory lay-offs.

option_analysis.label: Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade
option_analysis.diagnosis: DPIIT (under Ministry of Commerce & Industry) handles industrial policy, FDI, startups, and WPI, not labor welfare disputes.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Industrial department distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: DPIIT promotes industry and trade, not labor disputes.

option_analysis.label: Labour Bureau
option_analysis.diagnosis: The Labour Bureau is the dedicated organization responsible for compiling statistics on industrial disputes, strikes, lockouts, closures, and lay-offs.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Direct institutional mandate testing.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Industrial disputes + closures + lay-offs = Labour Bureau (Ministry of Labour).

option_analysis.label: National Technical Manpower Information System
option_analysis.diagnosis: NTMIS (under AICTE / Ministry of Education) tracks technical education graduates and engineering manpower demand.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Obscure technical manpower agency distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: NTMIS tracks technical graduates, not factory disputes.

subject: Polity & Governance
sub_topic: Statutory Bodies - Coal Controller's Organization
question_text:
In India, what is the role of the Coal Controller's Organization (CCO)?
1. CCO is the major source of Coal Statistics in Government of India.
2. It monitors progress of the development of Captive Coal/Lignite blocks.
3. It hears any objection to the Government’s notification relating to acquisition of coal-bearing areas.
4. It ensures that coal mining companies deliver the coal to end users in the prescribed time.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
explanation:
The Coal Controller's Organization (CCO) is a subordinate office under the Ministry of Coal with established statutory functions:
1. Under the Collection of Statistics Act, 2008, CCO collects and publishes the definitive statistical yearbook 'Coal Directory of India' and 'Provisional Coal Statistics', serving as the primary source of all official coal data for the Government of India. Statement 1 is correct.
2. CCO monitors the milestone-wise progress and development of all allocated captive and commercial coal and lignite mining blocks across the country. Statement 2 is correct.
3. Under Section 8 of the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, the Coal Controller is statutory designated to hear, examine, and adjudicate upon any objections raised by landowners and stakeholders against government notifications to acquire coal-bearing land, and submits his report to the Central Government. Statement 3 is correct.
4. CCO is a regulatory and statistical body; it does NOT manage commercial coal supply logistics or enforce delivery deadlines for coal mining companies to end-users (that is handled under commercial Fuel Supply Agreements - FSAs). Statement 4 is incorrect.
Therefore, 1, 2, and 3 are correct.
standard_book_ref: Coal Controller's Organization (CCO) Official Portal (coalcontroller.gov.in); Ministry of Coal Annual Report; Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957.
elimination_trap: Ensuring commercial delivery schedules to end-users (statement 4) is a micro-commercial/contractual obligation between buyers and sellers (e.g. Coal India Ltd and power plants), not a regulatory function of the Coal Controller. Eliminating statement 4 immediately removes (b) and (d). Statement 3 is an explicit statutory power under the 1957 Act, confirming (a) 1, 2 and 3.

mains_linkage.question: Examine the regulatory architecture of India's mineral and energy sectors, highlighting the statutory role of the Coal Controller's Organization amidst the commercialization of coal mining.

option_analysis.label: 1, 2 and 3
option_analysis.diagnosis: Statements 1, 2, and 3 are correct statutory functions of CCO (primary coal statistics, captive block monitoring, and hearing land acquisition objections under CBA Act 1957).
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Deep testing of a niche regulatory agency that hit headlines during captive coal block auctions.
option_analysis.mental_filter: CCO does statistics, captive monitoring, and land objections; commercial delivery schedules are not its job.

option_analysis.label: 3 and 4 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits statements 1 and 2 while accepting commercial delivery regulation in statement 4.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Distorts CCO into a commercial logistics controller.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Statement 4 is false.

option_analysis.label: 1 and 2 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits statement 3. Candidates often do not realize the Coal Controller acts as a statutory hearing authority under the 1957 Act.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Conservative option excluding quasi-judicial functions.
option_analysis.mental_filter: CCO explicitly hears objections under CBA Act 1957.

option_analysis.label: 1, 2 and 4
option_analysis.diagnosis: Accepts false commercial statement 4 while dropping the statutory land acquisition power.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Plausible combination for candidates guessing delivery management.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Delivery schedule enforcement is outside CCO's purview.

subject: Polity & Governance
sub_topic: Constitutional Framework - Fifth Schedule Areas
question_text: If a particular area is brought under the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements best reflects the consequence of it?
options: This would prevent the transfer of land of tribal people to non-tribal people.
This would create a local self-governing body in that area.
This would convert that area into a Union Territory.
The State having such areas would be declared a Special Category State.
explanation: Paragraph 5(2) of the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution of India explicitly empowers the Governor of a State to make regulations to prohibit or restrict the transfer of land by or among members of the Scheduled Tribes in such areas, and regulate the allotment of land to members of the STs. In the landmark judgment Samatha vs. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997), the Supreme Court ruled that tribal land in Fifth Schedule areas cannot be transferred, leased, or assigned to non-tribal individuals or even private corporations for mining or commercial activity, ensuring absolute protection of tribal land rights.
standard_book_ref: Indian Polity by M. Laxmikanth, Chapter 41: Scheduled and Tribal Areas; Constitution of India (Fifth Schedule); Samatha vs State of Andhra Pradesh (1997).
elimination_trap: Autonomous District Councils (local self-governing bodies) are created under the SIXTH Schedule (Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram), not the Fifth Schedule (which provides for Tribes Advisory Councils). Fifth Schedule fundamentally protects tribal land rights from non-tribal alienation.

mains_linkage.question: Differentiate between the constitutional safeguards provided under the Fifth and Sixth Schedules of the Indian Constitution, highlighting the role of the Governor in protecting tribal land alienation.

option_analysis.label: This would prevent the transfer of land of tribal people to non-tribal people.
option_analysis.diagnosis: The primary legal and constitutional protection under Para 5(2) of Fifth Schedule is prohibiting and restricting the transfer of tribal land to non-tribal persons.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Core constitutional provision testing based on landmark jurisprudence (Samatha case).
option_analysis.mental_filter: Fifth Schedule core mandate = prevent alienation of tribal land to non-tribals.

option_analysis.label: This would create a local self-governing body in that area.
option_analysis.diagnosis: Autonomous District Councils with legislative and judicial powers are created under the Sixth Schedule, not the Fifth Schedule.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Confuses Fifth Schedule (TACs) with Sixth Schedule (Autonomous District Councils).
option_analysis.mental_filter: Autonomous councils are Sixth Schedule.

option_analysis.label: This would convert that area into a Union Territory.
option_analysis.diagnosis: Scheduled areas remain part of their respective States; they are not turned into Union Territories.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Absurd administrative reorganization distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Scheduled areas do not become Union Territories.

option_analysis.label: The State having such areas would be declared a Special Category State.
option_analysis.diagnosis: Special Category Status was an economic classification accorded by the National Development Council based on Gadgil-Mukherjee formula, unrelated to the Fifth Schedule.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Fiscal federalism distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Fifth schedule does not grant Special Category State status.

subject: Polity & Governance
sub_topic: Institutions & Platforms - Urban Development & Sanitation
question_text:
Consider the following statements:
1. The India Sanitation Coalition is a platform to promote sustainable sanitation and is funded by the Government of India and the World Health Organization.
2. The National Institute of Urban Affairs is an apex body of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs in Government of India and provides innovative solutions for address the challenges of Urban India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation:
1. The India Sanitation Coalition (ISC) is a multi-stakeholder platform launched in 2015 at the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI). It is funded and supported by private organizations, foundations, and donors (such as the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, FICCI, and corporate CSR funds), NOT funded by the Government of India and the World Health Organization. Statement 1 is incorrect.
2. The National Institute of Urban Affairs (NIUA) was established in 1976 as an autonomous body registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1960. While it acts as a premier think-tank providing research and capacity-building support to the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, it is NOT an 'apex body of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs' (it is an independent registered society/think-tank). Statement 2 is incorrect.
Therefore, neither 1 nor 2 is correct.
standard_book_ref: National Institute of Urban Affairs (NIUA) Official Charter; India Sanitation Coalition Portal; Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs Annual Reports.
elimination_trap: Statement 1 falsely claims funding by GoI and WHO (it is a FICCI-hosted CSR/foundation platform). Statement 2 mischaracterizes an autonomous research society (NIUA) as an 'apex body of the Ministry'. Both statements contain subtle organizational distortions, making (d) Neither 1 nor 2 the official correct answer.

mains_linkage.question: Examine the role of autonomous think-tanks and public-private platforms in shaping urban governance reforms and sustainable sanitation policies in India.

option_analysis.label: 1 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: ISC is anchored at FICCI and funded by philanthropic foundations like BMGF, not GoI and WHO.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Fictitious government/UN funding claim.
option_analysis.mental_filter: ISC is a private/philanthropic coalition at FICCI.

option_analysis.label: 2 only
option_analysis.diagnosis: NIUA is an autonomous research society registered under Societies Registration Act, not an official ministerial 'apex body'.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Exaggerates an autonomous think-tank's legal status.
option_analysis.mental_filter: NIUA is an independent think-tank society, not a ministry apex body.

option_analysis.label: Both 1 and 2
option_analysis.diagnosis: Accepts both plausible-sounding organizational profiles without verifying legal/funding status.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Lures candidates assuming official-sounding institutions must be accurately described.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Both institutional profiles contain factual errors.

option_analysis.label: Neither 1 nor 2
option_analysis.diagnosis: Both statements are factually incorrect regarding founding, legal status, and funding sources.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Double-negative institutional elimination.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Neither statement is factually accurate.

subject: Environment & Ecology
sub_topic: Environmental Legislation - Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
question_text: Which one of the following has been constituted under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986?
explanation:
The Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) was constituted under Section 3(3) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, following directions issued by the Supreme Court of India in the landmark case of M.C. Mehta vs. Union of India (1997). The Authority is mandated to regulate, control, and manage ground water extraction and development across the country, with statutory powers to notify over-exploited assessment units and impose environmental compensation.
- Central Water Commission (CWC) was established in 1945 by executive resolution.
- Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) is a subordinate technical office under the Ministry of Jal Shakti, established in 1970.
- National Water Development Agency (NWDA) was set up in 1982 as an autonomous registered society for the Interlinking of Rivers project.
standard_book_ref: Indian Polity by M. Laxmikanth - Environmental Authorities; PMFIAS Environment - Environmental Acts and Policies; Central Ground Water Authority Official Portal.
elimination_trap: Carefully distinguish between Central Ground Water Board (CGWB - a technical wing created in 1970) and Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA - a statutory regulatory body created under EPA 1986 pursuant to the M.C. Mehta judgment).

mains_linkage.question: Evaluate the regulatory efficacy of the Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) in arresting alarming groundwater depletion rates in northwestern India.

option_analysis.label: Central Water Commission
option_analysis.diagnosis: Established in 1945 as an attached technical office by executive order, long predating the EPA 1986.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Premier national surface water technical body.
option_analysis.mental_filter: CWC dates back to 1945.

option_analysis.label: Central Ground Water Board
option_analysis.diagnosis: Formed in 1970 by renaming the Exploratory Tube-wells Organization; it is an executive subordinate office, not constituted under EPA 1986.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Direct phonetic trap with Central Ground Water Authority.
option_analysis.mental_filter: CGWB is a 1970 technical board, not the EPA statutory body.

option_analysis.label: Central Ground Water Authority
option_analysis.diagnosis: CGWA was explicitly constituted under Section 3(3) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 following Supreme Court orders.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Standard legal authority origin testing.
option_analysis.mental_filter: EPA 1986 Section 3(3) created the Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA).

option_analysis.label: National Water Development Agency
option_analysis.diagnosis: Constituted in 1982 as an autonomous society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: River-linking agency distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: NWDA is an autonomous society created in 1982.

subject: Polity & Governance
sub_topic: International Bodies - UN Credentials Committee
question_text:
With reference to the "United Nations Credentials Committee", consider the following statements:
1. It is a committee set up by the UN Security Council and works under its supervision.
2. It traditionally meets in March, June and September every year.
3. It assesses the credentials of all UN members before submitting a report to the General Assembly for approval.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation:
1. Under Rule 28 of the Rules of Procedure of the UN General Assembly, the Credentials Committee is appointed by the General Assembly at the beginning of each regular session, NOT by the UN Security Council. It consists of nine members appointed by the General Assembly upon the proposal of the President. Statement 1 is incorrect.
2. The Committee does not follow a rigid quarterly calendar of March, June, and September.
