elimination_trap: High-difficulty factual question testing post-independence trade unionism. B.P. Wadia founded Madras Labour Union (1918); Lala Lajpat Rai and N.M. Joshi were associated with AITUC (1920); C.P. Ramaswamy Iyer was a princely diwan.

mains_linkage.question: Trace the evolution of the Indian trade union movement from the inter-war period to the immediate post-independence era, noting ideological divergences.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: B.P. Wadia founded the Madras Labour Union (1918); he was not associated with the 1948 Hind Mazdoor Sabha.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Mixes early 1918 labour pioneer B.P. Wadia into a post-independence organization.
option_analysis.mental_filter: B.P. Wadia belongs to 1918, not 1948.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Sir C.P. Ramaswamy Iyer was the Diwan of Travancore, not a socialist trade unionist.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Includes a conservative princely administrator.
option_analysis.mental_filter: C.P. Ramaswamy Iyer was Diwan of Travancore, completely unrelated to trade unions.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: N.M. Joshi was the principal architect and general secretary of AITUC in 1920.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Associates AITUC's founding father with HMS.
option_analysis.mental_filter: N.M. Joshi founded AITUC, not HMS.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: Ashok Mehta, T.S. Ramanujam, and G.G. Mehta were the socialist founders of the Hind Mazdoor Sabha in 1948.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Precision factual question distinguishing socialist trade unionists from Congress and communist union leaders.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Hind Mazdoor Sabha (1948) = Socialist leaders (Ashok Mehta, G.G. Mehta, T.S. Ramanujam).

subject: History & Culture
sub_topic: Ancient Indian Religions - Jainism (Sthanakvasi Sect)
question_text: With reference to the religious practices in India, the "Sthanakvasi" sect belongs to
explanation:
The 'Sthanakvasi' is a prominent sub-sect of the Svetambara tradition in Jainism.
It was founded by a merchant named Lavaji around 1653 AD (derived from the earlier 15th-century Lonka Shaha reform movement). The defining spiritual feature of the Sthanakvasis is their rejection of idol worship (murti-puja) and temple rituals. Instead of worshipping images of Tirthankaras in ornate stone temples, they perform meditation, contemplation, and prayers in unadorned prayer halls known as 'Sthanakas'. Sthanakvasi monks also wear a white cloth mask (Muhapatti) over their mouth at all times to prevent harming airborne microscopic organisms.
standard_book_ref: NCERT Class XI - An Introduction to Indian Art; AL Basham - The Wonder That Was India; Romila Thapar
elimination_trap: Candidates often confuse Buddhist schools (Theravada, Mahayana, Hinayana, Vajrayana) with Jain sub-sects (Digambara: Bisapantha, Terapantha; Svetambara: Murtipujaka, Sthanakvasi, Terapanthi). Sthanakvasi is strictly Jain.

mains_linkage.question: Examine the philosophical debates and reform movements within Jainism that led to the emergence of aniconic sects like the Sthanakvasi.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Buddhism has schools like Sautrantika, Vaibhashika, Sthaviravada, but Sthanakvasi is not Buddhist.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Lures candidates familiar with Buddhist monastic terms into misclassifying a Jain sect.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Sthanakvasi is not Buddhist.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: Sthanakvasi is an iconic-rejecting Svetambara sect of Jainism founded in the 17th century.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Standard religious sect identification testing detailed knowledge of Indian religions.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Sthanakvasi = Svetambara Jain sect (praying in Sthanakas, no idol worship).

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Shaivism includes sects like Pasupata, Kapalika, Kalamukha, Kashmir Shaivism, and Lingayatism.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Hindu sectarian distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Sthanakvasi has no connection to Shaiva sects.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Vaishnavism comprises sects like Sri Vaishnavism, Gaudiya, Pushtimarg, and Nimbarka.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Hindu devotional tradition distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Vaishnavism is murti-centric, unlike Sthanakvasi.

subject: History & Culture
sub_topic: Mughal and Awadhi Architecture - Building Materials & Techniques
question_text:
With reference to the cultural history of India, consider the following statements :
• White marble was used in making Buland Darwaza and Khankah at Fatehpur Sikri.
• Red sandstone and marble were used in making Bara Imambara and Rumi Darwaza at Lucknow.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation:
Evaluating the architectural materials used in these monumental structures:
1. Statement 1 is incorrect: The Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri (built by Akbar in 1601 to commemorate his victory over Gujarat) is constructed predominantly of red and buff sandstone, with white and black marble used sparingly as decorative inlay on the spandrels and borders—not as the primary structural material. Similarly, the Khankah (hospice of Sheikh Salim Chishti) was built in red sandstone (though Salim Chishti's separate tomb inside was later cased in white marble by Jahangir).
2. Statement 2 is incorrect: In the Awadh region (Lucknow), there were no nearby quarries of sandstone or marble. Consequently, Nawabi architecture utilized local materials: the Bara Imambara (built by Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula in 1784) and the Rumi Darwaza are constructed of thin 'Lakhori' bricks bonded with lime-surkhi mortar and finished with elaborate fine stucco (lime plaster) ornamentation. No red sandstone or marble was used in their construction.
Therefore, neither statement 1 nor statement 2 is correct.
standard_book_ref: NCERT Class XI - An Introduction to Indian Art (Mughal and Regional Architecture); Percy Brown - Indian Architecture (Islamic Period)
elimination_trap: Candidates frequently associate grand Islamic monuments generically with 'red sandstone and marble'. However, Lucknow's Awadhi architecture is uniquely characterized by brick-and-stucco, devoid of stone quarries. Thus statement 2 is false, and statement 1 falsely claims Buland Darwaza was made of white marble.

mains_linkage.question: Compare the architectural styles and structural materials of the Imperial Mughal monuments of Fatehpur Sikri with the Nawabi architecture of Lucknow.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Buland Darwaza's primary building material is red sandstone, not white marble.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Confuses decorative inlay with primary construction material.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Buland Darwaza is red sandstone.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Bara Imambara and Rumi Darwaza contain no red sandstone or marble; they are built of Lakhori brick and lime stucco.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Transposes Agra/Delhi stone traditions onto brick-and-stucco Awadhi architecture.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Lucknow monuments are built of Lakhori bricks, not stone/marble.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Both statements contain fundamental architectural inaccuracies.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Dual acceptance trap for casual observers.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Both statements misstate the primary materials.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: Neither statement is correct: Buland Darwaza is sandstone (not marble), and Bara Imambara is brick-stucco (not stone/marble).
option_analysis.examiner_craft: High-level material culture question testing structural fabric of historic monuments.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Neither 1 nor 2 is correct.

subject: History & Culture
sub_topic: Medieval Foreign Travellers - Jean-Baptiste Tavernier & Diamond Mines
question_text: Which one of the following foreign travellers elaborately discussed about diamonds and diamond mines of India?
explanation:
Jean-Baptiste Tavernier was a 17th-century French gem merchant and traveller who made six extensive voyages to Persia and India between 1630 and 1668.
Being a professional jeweller and gemologist, Tavernier's travelogue ('Les Six Voyages de Jean-Baptiste Tavernier') provides an exceptionally detailed, firsthand technical and commercial description of India's diamond mines, notably the Golconda mines at Kollur (where he inspected the Koh-i-Noor and purchased the Great Blue Diamond, later known as the French Blue/Hope Diamond) and the Raolconda diamond mines.
In contrast, François Bernier was a French physician who wrote on Mughal politics and society; Jean de Thévenot was an explorer who documented flora, customs, and ports; Abbé Barthélemy Carré was a French Catholic priest.
standard_book_ref: NCERT Class XII - Themes in Indian History Part II (Chapter: Through the Eyes of Travellers); Satish Chandra - Medieval India
elimination_trap: Candidates often confuse François Bernier with Tavernier since both were French contemporaries during Aurangzeb's reign; but Bernier was a physician focused on landownership and oriental despotism, while Tavernier was the jeweler who specialized in diamonds.

mains_linkage.question: Discuss the historical value and limitations of 17th-century European travelogues (such as Bernier and Tavernier) in reconstructing the socioeconomic conditions of Mughal India.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: François Bernier was a physician to Prince Dara Shikoh and later Aurangzeb; he analyzed political systems and absence of private property in land.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Classic Bernier vs Tavernier French contemporary trap.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Bernier = Physician; Tavernier = Jewel merchant.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: Jean-Baptiste Tavernier was a gem merchant who extensively documented Golconda's diamond mines.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Direct traveler-specialization recall testing the vocational focus of European visitors.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Tavernier = Diamonds and precious stones of India.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Jean de Thévenot travelled in Gujarat and the Deccan, focusing on botanical specimens and administrative governance, not mining engineering.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Obscure French traveller distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Thévenot did not specialize in diamond trade.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Abbé Barthélemy Carré was a Catholic priest and diplomatic envoy for Colbert's French East India Company.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Clerical traveller distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Carré was a diplomatic priest, not a diamond expert.

subject: History & Culture
sub_topic: Buddhism - Bodhisattvas & Maitreya Buddha
question_text: With reference to Indian history, who among the following is a future Buddha, yet to come to save the world?
explanation:
In Buddhist eschatology across both Theravada and Mahayana traditions, 'Maitreya' is the prophesied future Buddha who is destined to appear on Earth in the next cosmic era (kalpa) when the teachings of Gautama Buddha (dharma) have completely eroded and been forgotten.
According to canonical texts, Maitreya currently resides as a Bodhisattva in the Tushita heaven waiting for the appropriate epoch to descend, achieve enlightenment, and preach the pure dharma to liberate humanity.
Regarding other Bodhisattvas:
- Avalokiteshvara (or Padmapani): Bodhisattva of infinite compassion who holds a lotus.
- Lokeshvara: Another manifestation of Avalokiteshvara as 'Lord of the World'.
standard_book_ref: NCERT Class XI - An Introduction to Indian Art; AL Basham - The Wonder That Was India; Upinder Singh
elimination_trap: Padmapani and Avalokiteshvara are the same Bodhisattva of Compassion; Maitreya is uniquely recognized as the future Buddha.

mains_linkage.question: Explain the theological evolution of the Bodhisattva concept in Mahayana Buddhism and its representation in ancient Indian art (such as Gandhara and Ajanta).

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Avalokiteshvara is the Bodhisattva of Compassion (holding lotus), not the prophesied future Buddha.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Confuses the most popular active Bodhisattva with the future Buddha.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Avalokiteshvara = Bodhisattva of Compassion.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Lokesvara ('Lord of the World') is an epithet/form of Avalokiteshvara.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Synonym trap for Avalokiteshvara.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Lokesvara is Avalokiteshvara.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: Maitreya is universally recognized in Buddhist canon as the future Buddha yet to come.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Direct canonical Buddhist doctrine recall.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Future Buddha = Maitreya.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Padmapani ('lotus bearer') is a specific depiction of Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara (e.g., Cave 1 at Ajanta).
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Famous iconographic representation of Avalokiteshvara.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Padmapani is the lotus-bearing Bodhisattva at Ajanta.

subject: History & Culture
sub_topic: British Expansionist Policies - Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance System
question_text: Which one of the following statements does not apply to the system of Subsidiary Alliance introduced by Lord Wellesley?
options: To maintain a large standing army at other’s expense
To keep India safe from Napoleonic danger
To secure a ﬁxed income for the Company
To establish British paramountcy over the Indian States
explanation:
The Subsidiary Alliance system, devised and perfected by Governor-General Lord Wellesley (1798–1805), was a diplomatic instrument of British imperialism with clear strategic objectives:
1. To maintain a large standing British military force in the heart of native states at the native ruler's expense (Applicable to Subsidiary Alliance).
2. To establish British paramountcy and prevent native states from allying with one another or employing other Europeans without British consent (Applicable).
3. To eliminate French intrigue and keep India safe from the threat of Napoleonic invasion (Applicable).

What did NOT apply was 'To secure a fixed income for the Company':
The financial arrangement under the Subsidiary Alliance required the Indian ruler either to pay an annual subsidy to maintain the British contingent or to cede territory in perpetuity whose revenue covered the troop costs. The objective was military deployment and imperial security at the cost of Indian princes, NOT generating a fixed budgetary revenue stream for the Company's coffers. Therefore, option C does not apply.
standard_book_ref: Spectrum - Modern India (Chapter: Expansion and Consolidation of British Power in India); Bipan Chandra - Modern India
elimination_trap: Notice the negative phrasing: 'does NOT apply'. The system was designed to establish political hegemony and military dominance at zero cost to the Company; it was not designed as an income-generating revenue tax instrument.

mains_linkage.question: Critically evaluate Lord Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance as an instrument of British paramountcy. How did it reduce Indian princely rulers to subordinate clients?

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Maintaining British subsidiary forces at other's expense was the core operative feature of the alliance.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Valid feature presented under a 'does NOT apply' prompt.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Stationing army at ruler's expense was the main feature.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Eliminating French influence and securing the frontier against Napoleon was Wellesley's explicit primary geopolitical motive in 1798.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Valid geopolitical motive.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Countering French influence was a primary aim.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: Securing a fixed income for the Company was NOT an objective; the alliance was a political-military mechanism to outsource defense costs and annex sovereign powers.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Tests deep understanding of the military-diplomatic intent of Wellesley vs fiscal taxation.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Subsidiary alliance was about military control, not securing fixed commercial revenue.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Establishing British paramountcy over Indian states was the overarching political goal realized by Wellesley.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Standard textbook goal of the alliance.
option_analysis.mental_filter: British paramountcy was the fundamental goal.

subject: History & Culture
sub_topic: Colonial Education Policy - Charter Act 1813 & Anglicist Controversy
question_text:
Which of the following led to the introduction of English Education in India?
• Charter Act of 1813
• General Committee of Public Instruction, 1823
• Orientalist and Anglicist Controversy
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
explanation:
All three factors played fundamental, consecutive roles in introducing English education in colonial India:
1. Charter Act of 1813: Section 43 of the Act set aside a financial allocation of one lakh rupees annually for the revival and improvement of literature, encouragement of learned natives, and introduction/promotion of knowledge of the sciences among inhabitants of British territories.
2. General Committee of Public Instruction (GCPI), 1823: Appointed by the colonial administration to oversee the disbursement and utilization of the annual educational grant sanctioned by the Charter Act of 1813.
3. Orientalist and Anglicist Controversy: Within the GCPI, sharp ideological cleavages arose between the Orientalists (led by H.T. Prinsep, advocating classical Persian, Arabic, and Sanskrit education) and the Anglicists (led by Charles Trevelyan, demanding modern western education in the English medium). This debate was decisively settled in 1835 by Lord Macaulay's famous Minute and William Bentinck's English Education Act of 1835.
Hence, 1, 2, and 3 all contributed directly.
standard_book_ref: Spectrum - Modern India (Chapter: Development of Modern Education); Bipan Chandra - Modern India
elimination_trap: Some candidates hesitate whether the GCPI of 1823 or the Charter Act of 1813 directly 'led' to English education since the formal decision came in 1835, but all three were the foundational institutional and legislative stepping stones.

mains_linkage.question: Trace the evolution of colonial education policy from the Charter Act of 1813 to Wood's Despatch of 1854, highlighting the ideological contest between Anglicists and Orientalists.

option_analysis.label: Partial
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits the GCPI 1823 and Anglicist controversy, which were the operational vehicles for English policy.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Tests if candidate connects legislative sanction with subsequent administrative execution.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Charter Act alone was not the sole factor.

option_analysis.label: Partial
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits the Anglicist-Orientalist debate that culminated in Macaulay's Minute.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Excludes the famous ideological controversy.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Anglicist controversy was the direct turning point.

option_analysis.label: Partial
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits Charter Act 1813 and GCPI 1823.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Singles out only the ideological controversy.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Charter Act of 1813 was the legal fountainhead.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: All three—Charter Act 1813, GCPI 1823, and Orientalist-Anglicist controversy—sequentially established English education in India.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Comprehensive historical causality question where all three elements formed the policy chain.
option_analysis.mental_filter: 1 (Charter 1813) + 2 (GCPI 1823) + 3 (Controversy) = 1, 2 and 3.

subject: Geography
sub_topic: Lakes & Water Bodies of India - Natural vs Artificial
question_text: Which one of the following is an ‘artiﬁcial lake‘?
explanation:
Evaluating the nature and origin of each lake:
1. Kodaikanal Lake (Tamil Nadu): A famous man-made, artificial star-shaped lake situated in the Palani Hills. It was created in 1863 by Sir Vere Henry Levinge, the former Collector of Madurai, by bunding and damming three natural streams flowing through the valley.
2. Kolleru Lake (Andhra Pradesh): A natural freshwater lake situated between the Godavari and Krishna river deltas.
3. Nainital Lake (Uttarakhand): A natural tectonic/freshwater lake situated in the Kumaon region of the outer Himalayas.
4. Renuka Lake (Himachal Pradesh): The largest natural freshwater lake in Himachal Pradesh, recognized as a Ramsar wetland site.
standard_book_ref: NCERT Class XI - India: Physical Environment (Chapter 3: Drainage System); Majid Husain - Geography of India
elimination_trap: Candidates often confuse natural tectonic hill station lakes (like Nainital and Renuka) with artificial colonial impoundments (like Kodaikanal). Kodaikanal was explicitly constructed as an artificial lake in 1863.

mains_linkage.question: Examine the ecological vulnerabilities of fragile hill-station water bodies in the Western Ghats and Himalayas under urban and tourism pressure.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: Kodaikanal Lake in Tamil Nadu is an artificial lake created in 1863 by damming three streams.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Distinguishes artificial colonial hill-station reservoirs from natural tectonic/deltaic lakes.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Kodaikanal is an artificial man-made lake created by Sir Vere Henry Levinge.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Kolleru is a natural deltaic freshwater lake between Krishna and Godavari.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Major natural wetland distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Kolleru is a natural lake.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Nainital is a natural crescent-shaped tectonic lake in the Himalayas.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Famous hill station lake distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Nainital is natural tectonic.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Renuka Lake in Sirmaur district is a natural lake and Ramsar site.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Ramsar wetland distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Renuka is a natural freshwater lake.

subject: Polity & Governance
sub_topic: Government Schemes - Skill Development (PMKVY)
question_text:
With reference to Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana, consider the following statements :
• It is the ﬂagship scheme of the Ministry of Labour and Employment.
• It, among other things, will also impart training in soft skills, entrepreneurship, ﬁnancial and digital literacy.
• It aims to align the competencies of the unregulated workforce of the country to the National Skill Qualiﬁcation Framework.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation:
Evaluating Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY):
1. Statement 1 is incorrect: PMKVY is the flagship outcome-based skill training scheme of the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE), launched in 2015 and executed through the National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC)—not the Ministry of Labour and Employment.
2. Statement 2 is correct: Along with technical industry skills, PMKVY provides mandatory training in soft skills, entrepreneurship, personal hygiene, and financial and digital literacy to enhance employability.
3. Statement 3 is correct: A flagship pillar of PMKVY is 'Recognition of Prior Learning' (RPL), which formally assesses and certifies the informal, experiential competencies of the unregulated, unorganized workforce against the National Skills Qualification Framework (NSQF).
standard_book_ref: MSDE Annual Reports; India Year Book (Chapter: Labour, Skill Development and Employment)
elimination_trap: Nodal Ministry trap: Statement 1 attributes PMKVY to the Ministry of Labour and Employment instead of MSDE. Eliminating statement 1 leaves only option C (2 and 3 only).

mains_linkage.question: Critically evaluate the performance of Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY) in bridging India's vocational skill gap and informal workforce certification.

option_analysis.label: Partial
option_analysis.diagnosis: Statement 1 is false (MSDE, not Labour Ministry). Omits statement 3.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Nodal ministry swap error.
option_analysis.mental_filter: PMKVY belongs to Skill Development Ministry, not Labour.

option_analysis.label: Partial
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits statement 3, which is the core RPL objective of PMKVY.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Under-inclusive distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: PMKVY definitely aligns skills to NSQF via RPL.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. PMKVY imparts soft skills and certifies existing informal competencies against the NSQF.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Classic nodal ministry elimination pattern: eliminating 1 isolates 2 and 3.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Eliminate Statement 1 -> C (2 and 3 only).

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Includes statement 1, which has the wrong ministry.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: All-inclusive trap.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Reject D due to Statement 1.

subject: History & Culture
sub_topic: National Movement - All India Home Rule League to Swarajya Sabha (1920)
question_text: In 1920, which of the following changed its name to "Swarajya Sabha" ?
explanation:
In 1920, the 'All India Home Rule League' (originally founded by Annie Besant and Bal Gangadhar Tilak in 1916) elected Mahatma Gandhi as its President.
Under Gandhi's leadership in October 1920, the organization revised its constitution and changed its name to 'Swarajya Sabha'. Its stated objective was amended to securing 'Purna Swaraj' (complete self-rule) for India by peaceful and legitimate means, aligning the organizational network of the Home Rule movement directly with the forthcoming Non-Cooperation Movement.
standard_book_ref: Bipan Chandra - India's Struggle for Independence (Chapter: Non-Cooperation Movement); Spectrum - Modern India
elimination_trap: High-yield historical fact: Candidates frequently guess the Servants of India Society or Hindu Mahasabha, but Gandhi specifically presided over the renamed All India Home Rule League as 'Swarajya Sabha' in 1920.

mains_linkage.question: Examine how Mahatma Gandhi channeled the institutional networks of the Home Rule Leagues into the mass struggle of the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1920.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: The All India Home Rule League adopted the name Swarajya Sabha in 1920 under Mahatma Gandhi's presidency.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Tests precise institutional transitions on the eve of the Non-Cooperation Movement.
option_analysis.mental_filter: All India Home Rule League -> renamed Swarajya Sabha in 1920.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: The Hindu Mahasabha (founded in 1915 by Madan Mohan Malaviya) retained its own distinct nomenclature.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Contemporary political organization distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Hindu Mahasabha was never named Swarajya Sabha.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: The South Indian Liberal Federation (Justice Party, founded in 1916) maintained its identity in Madras Presidency.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Regional non-Brahmin movement distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: SILF became the Justice Party, not Swarajya Sabha.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: The Servants of India Society (founded by Gopal Krishna Gokhale in 1905) remained active under Srinivasa Sastri and never changed its name.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Moderate political society distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Servants of India Society remained distinct.

subject: History & Culture
sub_topic: Chronology of Modern Indian History & Literature
question_text: Which among the following events happened earliest?
options: Satyendranath Tagore became the first Indian to succeed in the Indian Civil Services Examination.
explanation:
Arranging the given historical events chronologically:
1. Dinabandhu Mitra wrote 'Neeldarpan' (Indigo Mirror): Written in 1858–1859 and published in 1860 in Dhaka, portraying the brutal oppression of Bengal indigo ryots by European planters during the Indigo Revolt.
2. Satyendranath Tagore cleared ICS: In June 1863, Satyendranath Tagore (elder brother of Rabindranath Tagore) became the first Indian to successfully qualify for the Indian Civil Services examination.
3. Swami Dayanand Saraswati established Arya Samaj: Founded on April 10, 1875, at Bombay to reform Vedic Hinduism.
4. Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote 'Anandmath': Published in 1882 (set in the context of the Sanyasi Rebellion, containing the national song 'Vande Mataram').
Therefore, the earliest event is Dinabandhu Mitra writing Neeldarpan (1858-1859).
standard_book_ref: Spectrum - Modern India (Chapters on Peasant Movements, Socio-Religious Reforms, and Civil Services); NCERT Class XII
elimination_trap: Indigo Revolt occurred immediately after the 1857 Revolt in 1859-60; Neeldarpan was written at the peak of the indigo rebellion (1858-59), making it comfortably earlier than the 1863 ICS, 1875 Arya Samaj, and 1882 Anandmath.

mains_linkage.question: Discuss the role of 19th-century vernacular literature—such as Dinabandhu Mitra's Neeldarpan and Bankim Chandra's Anandmath—in awakening anti-colonial national consciousness.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Arya Samaj was established in 1875 in Bombay, much later than Neeldarpan (1858-59).
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Socio-religious milestone dating distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Arya Samaj = 1875.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: Neeldarpan was composed in 1858–59 during the Indigo Revolt, making it the earliest of the four events.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Comparative chronology testing exact literary-historical milestones of 19th-century India.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Neeldarpan (1858-59) is the earliest.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Anandmath was published in 1882, the latest among all four options.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Famous patriotic novel distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Anandmath = 1882.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Satyendranath Tagore passed the ICS exam in 1863, after Neeldarpan (1858-59).
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Pioneer achievement milestone distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Satyendranath Tagore ICS = 1863.

subject: Environment & Ecology
sub_topic: Environmental Degradation - Riverbed Sand Mining Impacts
question_text:
Which of the following is/are the possible consequence/s of heavy sand mining in riverbeds ?
• Decreased salinity in the river
• Pollution of groundwater
• Lowering of the water-table
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
explanation:
Evaluating the ecological and hydrological consequences of excessive riverbed sand mining:
1. Statement 1 is incorrect: Sand mining destabilizes the riverbed morphology and causes bed degradation/deepening. In coastal and estuarine zones, lower riverbeds allow sea water to push further inland during high tides, leading to salinity intrusion and INCREASING the salinity of river water, not decreasing it.
2. Statement 2 is correct: Sand beds act as natural mechanical, chemical, and biological filters that purify surface water as it percolates down into subterranean aquifers. Stripping away riverbed sand exposes the unconfined aquifer to direct surface runoff, agricultural chemicals, and pathogens, causing severe groundwater pollution.
3. Statement 3 is correct: Sand mining lowers the riverbed level, creating a steeper hydraulic gradient that accelerates drainage of water from adjoining riparian floodplains and alluvial banks into the deepened channel. This leads to a drastic lowering of the groundwater table across nearby agricultural lands.
Hence, 2 and 3 are the valid consequences.
standard_book_ref: PMFIAS - Environmental Pollution; MoEFCC Enforcement & Monitoring Guidelines for Sand Mining; Down To Earth
elimination_trap: Directional logic in Statement 1: It says 'salinity of river is decreased', whereas removal of sand allows seawater backflow and increases salinity. Eliminating statement 1 immediately eliminates options A and D, narrowing down to B or C.

mains_linkage.question: Examine the hydro-geomorphological and environmental consequences of unregulated riverbed sand mining in India. Suggest policy and technological interventions to regulate it.

option_analysis.label: Partial
option_analysis.diagnosis: Statement 1 is scientifically inverted (sand mining increases salinity via seawater intrusion).
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Reverses the direction of salinity change to test hydrological understanding.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Riverbed mining increases salinity, not decreases.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: Statements 2 and 3 are genuine consequences: sand mining degrades natural aquifer filtration (causing pollution) and drops regional water tables.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Standard environmental degradation causal reasoning.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Statement 1 is false; 2 and 3 are true.

option_analysis.label: Partial
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits statement 3, which is a universally documented effect of river incisive mining.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Under-inclusive distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Lowering of water table is a direct consequence.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Includes statement 1, which states decreased salinity.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: All-inclusive trap.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Reject 1 -> Reject D.

subject: Geography
sub_topic: Soil Properties, Biogeochemical Cycles & Land Degradation
question_text:
With reference to agricultural soils, consider the following statements :
• A high content of organic matter in soil drastically reduces its water holding capacity.
• Soil does not play any role in the sulphur cycle.
• Irrigation over a period of time can contribute to the salinization of some agricultural lands.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
explanation:
Evaluating the statements regarding agricultural soils:
1. Statement 1 is incorrect: Soil organic matter (humus) has an extremely high water-retention capacity (behaving like a sponge, holding several times its own dry weight in moisture) and improves soil structural porosity. Therefore, high organic matter content substantially INCREASES (not drastically reduces) soil water holding capacity.
2. Statement 2 is incorrect: Soil plays a vital, central role in the global sulphur cycle. Organic sulphur stored in soil humus constitutes over 90% of total soil sulphur in non-calcareous soils, which soil microorganisms mineralize into plant-available sulphate (SO4^2-) ions through immobilization, mineralization, and oxidation-reduction reactions.
3. Statement 3 is correct: Prolonged irrigation, particularly flood irrigation in arid and semi-arid tracts with poor subsurface drainage, raises the groundwater table. As water evaporates rapidly under high solar radiation, dissolved mineral salts are drawn upward via capillary action and deposited in the topsoil, causing extensive secondary soil salinization and alkalinization (as observed in canal-irrigated parts of Punjab and Haryana).
Hence, only statement 3 is correct.
standard_book_ref: NCERT Class XI - India: Physical Environment (Chapter 6: Soils); D.K. Das - Introductory Soil Science
elimination_trap: Statement 1 claims organic matter 'drastically reduces' water holding capacity, which is the exact opposite of basic soil agronomy. Statement 2 uses the extreme absolute phrase 'does not play ANY role'. Eliminating 1 and 2 leaves B (3 only).

mains_linkage.question: Analyze the causes of secondary soil salinization in the intensively irrigated agricultural regions of northwest India. What agronomic practices can reverse this degradation?

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Statements 1 and 2 are both factually and scientifically incorrect.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Pairs two false statements against candidates who lack basic soil science knowledge.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Organic matter increases water holding; soil is central to sulphur cycle.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: Only statement 3 is correct: irrigation in dry areas causes capillary upward movement of salts leading to salinization.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Double extreme-statement elimination question (Statements 1 and 2 contain extreme negations/inversions).
option_analysis.mental_filter: Statements 1 and 2 are false -> only 3 is correct.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Statement 1 is false as organic matter enhances water retention.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Includes the inverted organic matter claim.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Organic matter never reduces water holding capacity.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Includes all statements, ignoring the clear scientific errors in 1 and 2.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: All-inclusive trap.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Reject 1 and 2.

subject: Environment & Ecology
sub_topic: International Environmental Governance - PAGE & Rio+20
question_text: The Partnership for Action on Green Economy (PAGE), a UN mechanim to assist countries transition towards greener and more inclusive economies, emerged at
options: The Earth Summit on Sustainable Development 2002, Johannesburg
The United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development 2012, Rio de Janeiro
The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change 2015, Paris
The World Sustainable Development Summit 2016, New Delhi
explanation:
The 'Partnership for Action on Green Economy' (PAGE) was launched in 2013 as a joint initiative of five United Nations agencies—UN Environment Programme (UNEP), International Labour Organization (ILO), UN Development Programme (UNDP), UN Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO), and UN Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR).
PAGE was created in direct response to the call at the United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development 2012 in Rio de Janeiro (UNCSD, popularly known as Rio+20), whose outcome document 'The Future We Want' called upon the UN system to assist interested member countries in transitioning toward inclusive green economies that foster economic growth, create decent jobs, eradicate poverty, and preserve ecological integrity.
standard_book_ref: UNEP Official Publications - PAGE Mechanism; Shankar IAS - Environment (Chapter: International Conventions)
elimination_trap: High-yield UN conference linkage: PAGE is specifically anchored in the Rio+20 Earth Summit of 2012 where the 'Green Economy in the context of sustainable development and poverty eradication' was one of the two core themes.

mains_linkage.question: Examine the role of international mechanisms like PAGE (Partnership for Action on Green Economy) in facilitating developing economies' transition to decarbonized growth.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: The 2002 World Summit on Sustainable Development (WSSD) in Johannesburg preceded the green economy UN mandate.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Ten-year earlier milestone summit distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Johannesburg 2002 did not launch PAGE.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: PAGE was formulated and launched in direct response to the Rio+20 United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development in 2012.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Direct treaty-mechanism alignment testing Rio+20 outcomes.
option_analysis.mental_filter: PAGE = UNCSD Rio+20 (2012).

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: UNFCCC COP21 in Paris 2015 focused on the legally binding Paris Agreement on climate change, not PAGE.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Famous 2015 Paris Climate Agreement distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Paris 2015 was UNFCCC COP21, not PAGE.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: TERI's World Sustainable Development Summit in New Delhi is an annual institutional summit, not the UN launching forum for PAGE.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: National sustainability conference distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: WSDS New Delhi is not a UN treaty conference.

subject: Science & Technology
sub_topic: Additive Manufacturing - 3D Printing Applications
question_text:
“3D printing” has applications in which of the following?
• Preparation of confectionery items
• Manufacture of bionic ears
• Automotive industry
• Reconstructive surgeries
• Data processing technologies
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
explanation:
3D printing (additive manufacturing) builds three-dimensional physical objects layer-by-layer from digital CAD models. Its versatile applications span all five given sectors:
1. Preparation of confectionery items: Food 3D printers extrude edible pastes (chocolate, sugar, purees, dough) into intricate geometrical confectionery designs.
2. Manufacture of bionic ears: Bio-printing combines living cell matrices with embedded silver nanoparticles/electronics to print functional bionic ears and auditory prosthetics.
3. Automotive industry: Extensively utilized for rapid prototyping, lightweight topological metal components, personalized interior tooling, and discontinued replacement parts.
4. Reconstructive surgeries: Surgeons print customized titanium and bioceramic implants, cranial plates, and anatomical models matching patient CT scans for reconstructive and maxillofacial surgery.
5. Data processing technologies: Utilized in printing microfluidic logic chips, micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS), multidimensional optical storage, and conductive circuitry for physical computing devices.
Hence, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 all represent valid applications.
standard_book_ref: Science Reporter; Department of Science & Technology (DST) Technology Vision 2035
elimination_trap: Aspirants might doubt 'data processing technologies' or 'confectionery items', but additive manufacturing is an expansive frontier tech whose applications routinely encompass all plausible domains.

mains_linkage.question: Discuss the transformative potential of 3D printing (additive manufacturing) in revolutionizing biomedical engineering and advanced manufacturing in India.

option_analysis.label: Partial
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits bionic ears and data processing technologies, both established 3D printing applications.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Conventional industrial-only distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: 3D printing is widely used in medicine and computing.

option_analysis.label: Partial
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits confectionery, reconstructive surgery, and computing.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Arbitrary sub-selection.
option_analysis.mental_filter: 3D printed food and surgery are prominent use cases.

option_analysis.label: Partial
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits automotive and confectionery.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Under-inclusive distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Automotive was one of the earliest adopters of 3D printing.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: All five domains—food/confectionery, bionics, automotive, surgery, and data processing—utilize 3D printing technologies.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Universal application question typical of emerging technology topics in UPSC.
option_analysis.mental_filter: All 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 are valid 3D printing applications.

subject: Geography
sub_topic: Physiography of India - Volcanism (Barren Island)
question_text:
Consider the following statements:
• The Barren Island volcano is an active volcano located in the Indian territory.
• Barren Island lies about 140 km east of Great Nicobar.
• The last time the Barren Island volcano erupted was in 1991 and it has remained inactive since then.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
explanation:
Evaluating the statements regarding Barren Island:
1. Statement 1 is correct: Barren Island, situated in the Andaman Sea, is the only confirmed active volcano in India and the entire South Asian region.
2. Statement 2 is incorrect: Barren Island lies in the Andaman group, approximately 138 km northeast of Port Blair (the capital of Andaman & Nicobar Islands). It is located hundreds of kilometres north of Great Nicobar (which is the southernmost island of the Nicobar group, separated by the Ten Degree Channel and Sombrero Channel), not 140 km east of it.
3. Statement 3 is incorrect: After remaining dormant for over a century, the Barren Island volcano erupted violently in 1991, but it did NOT remain inactive thereafter. It erupted repeatedly in 1994–95, 2005, 2008, 2011, and had another major eruptive episode in January–February 2017 (reported widely by the Geological Survey of India and NIO).
Therefore, only statement 1 is correct.
standard_book_ref: NCERT Class XI - India: Physical Environment (Chapter 2: Structure and Physiography); Geological Survey of India (GSI) Bulletins
elimination_trap: Statement 3 claims the volcano 'has remained inactive since 1991'. Barren Island was in national headlines in early 2017 when scientists from the National Institute of Oceanography (NIO) documented it spewing ash and lava.

mains_linkage.question: Describe the tectonic framework of the Andaman and Nicobar ridge system and the geodynamic mechanisms driving active volcanism at Barren Island.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: Only statement 1 is correct: Barren Island is India's only active volcano. Statements 2 and 3 contain geographical and chronological errors.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Pairs a well-known basic physical fact with specific location and recency distractors.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Barren Island is an active Indian volcano; it lies NE of Port Blair and erupted recently (2017).

option_analysis.label: Partial
option_analysis.diagnosis: Statement 2 is false as Barren Island is near Port Blair, far north of Great Nicobar.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Swaps Port Blair with Great Nicobar to test map precision.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Barren Island is in the Andaman group, not near Great Nicobar.

option_analysis.label: Partial
option_analysis.diagnosis: Statement 3 is false because the volcano erupted multiple times after 1991 (notably 2017).
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Exploits lack of recent news awareness regarding post-1991 eruptions.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Barren Island erupted repeatedly, including in 2017.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Statements 2 and 3 are both factually incorrect.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Catch-all distractor for incorrect statements.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Only 1 is correct.

subject: Environment & Ecology
sub_topic: Invasive Alien Species - Prosopis juliflora
question_text: Why is a plant called Prosopis juliﬂora often mentioned in news?
options: Its extract is widely used in cosmetics.
It tends to reduce the biodiversity in the area in which it grows.
Its extract is used in the synthesis of pesticides.
explanation:
Prosopis juliflora (commonly known as Vilayati Kikar in Hindi or Seemai Karuvelam in Tamil) is a thorny shrub/tree native to Central and South America.
It was introduced to India in the 19th and early 20th centuries for afforestation, soil stabilization, and firewood in arid and semi-arid zones. However, it turned out to be an aggressive invasive alien species. It produces allelopathic chemicals that inhibit the germination of native vegetation, has an exceptionally deep taproot system that severely depletes local groundwater tables, and forms dense monospecific thickets that decimate native flora and fauna, drastically reducing local biodiversity.
standard_book_ref: PMFIAS - Biodiversity (Chapter: Invasive Alien Species); Shankar IAS - Environment; Madras High Court Judgments on Seemai Karuvelam eradication
elimination_trap: Widely publicized in environmental news and court cases (e.g. Tamil Nadu High Court directives to eradicate Prosopis juliflora due to severe ecological and groundwater damage). Clearly an invasive biodiversity threat.

mains_linkage.question: Examine the ecological and socioeconomic hazards posed by invasive alien species like Prosopis juliflora and Lantana camara in India's forest and grassland ecosystems.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Prosopis juliflora has no commercial application in high-end cosmetics.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Commercial botanical distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Vilayati Kikar is an ecological menace, not a cosmetic ingredient.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: It is an aggressive invasive alien species that outcompetes native flora, depletes groundwater, and degrades biodiversity.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Standard identification of prominent invasive alien plant species.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Prosopis juliflora = Invasive alien plant reducing local biodiversity.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Pesticide synthesis relies on neem (azadirachtin) or synthetic chemicals, not Prosopis juliflora.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Biopesticide distractor (confusing with neem).
option_analysis.mental_filter: It is not used to synthesize pesticides.

option_analysis.label: Incorrect
option_analysis.diagnosis: Option B provides the accurate, widely accepted ecological reason.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Residual option.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Option B is clearly correct.

subject: Environment & Ecology
sub_topic: Marine Ecosystems - Coral Reefs Distribution & Biodiversity
question_text:
Consider the following statements :
• Most of the world’s coral reefs are in tropical waters.
• More than one—third of the world’s coral reefs are located in the territories of Australia, Indonesia and Philippines.
• Coral reefs host far more number of animal phyla than those hosted by tropical rainforests.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
explanation:
Evaluating the statements regarding coral reefs:
1. Statement 1 is correct: Reef-building (hermatypic) corals have an obligate symbiotic relationship with photosynthetic zooxanthellae algae, requiring warm, clear, shallow, and saline waters with temperatures typically between 20°C and 30°C. Consequently, the vast majority of the world's coral reefs are concentrated in tropical waters between the Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn.
2. Statement 2 is correct: Over 33% (more than one-third) of the global coral reef area is located within the maritime boundaries of just three nations: Australia (home to the Great Barrier Reef), Indonesia, and the Philippines (the latter two forming the core of the Coral Triangle biodiversity hotspot).
3. Statement 3 is correct: Coral reefs are often termed the 'rainforests of the sea' due to their astonishing biodiversity. While tropical rainforests contain immense species richness within a few phyla (dominated overwhelmingly by insects/arthropods), coral reefs host far more animal phyla: 32 of the 34 recognized multicellular animal phyla are represented on coral reefs, compared to only about 9 phyla found in tropical rainforests.
Hence, 1, 2, and 3 are all correct.
standard_book_ref: PMFIAS - Aquatic Ecosystems: Coral Reefs; Shankar IAS - Environment; Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN) Reports
elimination_trap: Aspirants might doubt statement 3, assuming tropical rainforests must have more of everything; however, rainforests have higher species diversity within few phyla, whereas marine coral reefs possess vastly higher phyletic diversity (fundamental body plans).

mains_linkage.question: Discuss the ecological significance of coral reefs and the multidimensional threats they face from ocean warming, acidification, and anthropogenic stressors.

option_analysis.label: Partial
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits statement 3, which is a verified fact of comparative marine biology (phylum-level richness).
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Preys on doubt regarding the 'animal phyla' comparison between reefs and rainforests.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Coral reefs harbor 32 animal phyla, rainforests only about 9.

option_analysis.label: Partial
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits statement 1, which is the foundational ecological condition of coral reef distribution.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Excludes the basic geography of tropical reefs.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Reefs are overwhelmingly tropical.

option_analysis.label: Partial
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits statement 2, which accurately reflects global reef distribution in Australia, Indonesia, and Philippines.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Excludes geographic concentration data.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Australia + Indonesia + Philippines exceed 1/3 of global reefs.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: All three statements are scientifically and geographically correct: tropical concentration, >1/3 in top 3 countries, and higher animal phyla representation than rainforests.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: High-level ecological synthesis testing global geography, spatial statistics, and comparative taxonomy.
option_analysis.mental_filter: All 1, 2, and 3 are correct.

subject: Environment & Ecology
sub_topic: Global Climate Action - UNFCCC Initiatives (Climate Neutral Now)
question_text: "Momentum for Change: Climate Neutral Now" is an initiative launched by
options: The Intergovernmental panel on Climate Change
explanation:
'Momentum for Change: Climate Neutral Now' is a global initiative launched in 2015 by the Secretariat of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).
It was introduced to accelerate the transition toward a climate-neutral world as envisioned under the Paris Agreement. The initiative encourages and assists organizations, corporations, governments, and individuals to calculate their carbon footprint, reduce greenhouse gas emissions wherever feasible, and compensate for unavoidable emissions using UN-certified carbon credits (Certified Emission Reductions - CERs).
standard_book_ref: UNFCCC Official Portal - Momentum for Change; Shankar IAS - Environment (Chapter: Climate Change Organizations)
elimination_trap: High-frequency UPSC question pattern: Matching specific climate slogans/campaigns with their UN parent agency. UNFCCC manages Paris Agreement implementation and carbon offsets, making it the launching body for Climate Neutral Now.

mains_linkage.question: Assess the efficacy of voluntary carbon compensation mechanisms and climate-neutrality pledges under the UNFCCC framework in achieving global net-zero targets.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: IPCC is an assessment body that synthesizes scientific research on climate change; it does not launch public advocacy or offsetting campaigns.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Scientific assessment body distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: IPCC conducts scientific assessments, not voluntary action campaigns.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: UNEP coordinates environmental activities (like Champions of the Earth), but Climate Neutral Now is an initiative of the UNFCCC Secretariat.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Leading UN environmental body distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Climate Neutral Now belongs directly to UNFCCC.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: Launched in 2015 by the UNFCCC Secretariat under its Momentum for Change umbrella to promote voluntary carbon measurement and offsetting.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Direct institutional initiative recall.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Climate Neutral Now = UNFCCC Secretariat.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: WMO focuses on atmospheric science, meteorological observation, and weather forecasting.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Meteorological agency distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: WMO is a meteorological agency.

subject: History & Culture
sub_topic: Colonial Education - Orientalist Institutions & Founders
question_text:
With reference to educational institutions during colonial rule in India, consider the following pairs:
Institution                                                     Founder
• Sanskrit College at Benaras                William Jones
• Calcutta Madarsa                                 Warren Hastings
• Fort William Arthur College                  Wellesley
Which of the pairs given above is/are correct ?
explanation:
Evaluating the colonial educational institutions and their founders:
1. Sanskrit College at Benaras: Established in 1791 by Jonathan Duncan, the British Resident at Benaras, to study and preserve Hindu religion, laws, and literature. Sir William Jones founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal in 1784, not Benaras Sanskrit College. (Pair 1 is incorrectly matched).
2. Calcutta Madarsa (Madrasa-i-Aliya): Founded in 1781 by Warren Hastings, the first Governor-General of Bengal, for the teaching of Muslim law and related Islamic subjects in Arabic and Persian to train officers and interpreters for British courts. (Pair 2 is correctly matched).
3. Fort William College: Established in 1800 at Calcutta by Governor-General Richard Wellesley (Lord Mornington) to train young British civil servants in Indian languages, customs, and laws. Arthur Wellesley (later the Duke of Wellington) was his younger brother who led military campaigns against Tipu Sultan and the Marathas, not the Governor-General who founded the college. (Pair 3 is incorrectly matched).
standard_book_ref: Spectrum - Modern India (Chapter: Development of Modern Education); Bipan Chandra - Modern India
elimination_trap: Pair 3 slyly lists 'Arthur Wellesley' instead of 'Richard Wellesley' (Lord Wellesley). Pair 1 attributes Benaras Sanskrit College to William Jones instead of Jonathan Duncan. Both are classic UPSC examiner traps.

mains_linkage.question: Examine the motives behind the establishment of early colonial educational institutions like Calcutta Madarsa, Benaras Sanskrit College, and Fort William College.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Pairs 1 and 2 are grouped together, but Benaras Sanskrit College was founded by Jonathan Duncan, not William Jones.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Attributes Benaras Sanskrit College to the more famous Orientalist scholar William Jones.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Benaras Sanskrit College = Jonathan Duncan (1791).

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: Only pair 2 is correctly matched. Warren Hastings founded the Calcutta Madarsa in 1781.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Catches two subtle name traps: William Jones for Jonathan Duncan, and Arthur Wellesley for Richard Wellesley.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Calcutta Madarsa = Warren Hastings. Fort William = Richard Wellesley.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Pair 1 is false (Duncan) and pair 3 is false (Richard Wellesley, not Arthur).
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Pairs two historically erroneous combinations.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Both 1 and 3 are incorrect.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Pair 3 is incorrect because Fort William College was founded by Richard Wellesley.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: All-inclusive distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Arthur Wellesley was the military general brother, not the founder Governor-General.

subject: Geography
sub_topic: World Geography & Geopolitical Regions in News
question_text:
Consider the following pairs :
Regions sometimes mentioned in news                                         Country
• Catalonia                                                                                  Spain
• Crimea                                                                                      Hungary
• Mindanao                                                                                  Philippines
• Oromia                                                                                      Nigeria
Which of the pairs given, above are correctly matched ?
explanation:
Evaluating the geopolitical regions frequently in the international news and their countries:
1. Catalonia: An autonomous community in northeastern Spain. It was in the news following a controversial independence referendum held in October 2017 and subsequent declaration of independence. (Pair 1 is correctly matched).
2. Crimea: A peninsula on the northern coast of the Black Sea. It was internationally recognized as part of Ukraine before being militarily occupied and annexed by the Russian Federation in 2014. It has no geographical connection to Hungary. (Pair 2 is incorrectly matched).
3. Mindanao: The second-largest island of the Philippines in the south, which witnessed major military clashes between Philippine armed forces and ISIS-affiliated Islamist militants (Abu Sayyaf and Maute groups) during the 2017 Battle of Marawi. (Pair 3 is correctly matched).
4. Oromia: The largest regional state of Ethiopia, inhabited by the Oromo ethnic group. It was in the news due to widespread civil rights protests against the Ethiopian federal government. It is located in the Horn of Africa, not Nigeria. (Pair 4 is incorrectly matched).
Therefore, pairs 1 and 3 are correctly matched.
standard_book_ref: The Hindu - World Affairs / International News; Map reading - World Geopolitics
elimination_trap: Crimea is world-famous as Ukraine/Russia, making its pairing with Hungary completely absurd. Eliminating pair 2 immediately removes options A and D. Oromia is in Ethiopia (East Africa), not Nigeria (West Africa).

mains_linkage.question: Analyze the factors driving contemporary sub-national separatist and autonomy movements across Europe (e.g. Catalonia) and Southeast Asia (e.g. Mindanao).

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Includes pair 2, which absurdly places Crimea in Hungary.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Blatant geographical mismatch distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Crimea is in Ukraine/Russia, not Hungary.

option_analysis.label: Partial
option_analysis.diagnosis: Omits Catalonia (Pair 1), which was the most prominent European geopolitical headline in 2017.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Under-inclusive distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Catalonia is definitely in Spain.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: Pairs 1 and 3 are correctly matched: Catalonia is in Spain, and Mindanao is in the Philippines.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Tests contemporary international conflict hotspots and geographical mapping.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Catalonia = Spain; Mindanao = Philippines. Pairs 1 and 3.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Pair 4 is incorrectly matched: Oromia is a regional state of Ethiopia, not Nigeria.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Swaps East African Ethiopia with West African Nigeria.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Oromia is in Ethiopia.

subject: History & Culture
sub_topic: Post-Independence India - Chronology of State Reorganization & Economic Milestones
question_text:
Consider the following events :
• The first democratically elected communist party government formed in a State in India.
• India's then largest bank, ‘Imperial Bank of India', was renamed ‘State Bank of India'.
• Air India was nationalised and became the national carrier.
• Goa became a part of independent India.
Which of the following is the correct chronological sequence of the above events?
explanation:
Establishing the exact chronological timeline of these post-independence milestones:
1. Nationalisation of Air India: In 1953, the Government of India passed the Air Corporations Act, 1953, nationalizing the domestic and international aviation industry, creating Indian Airlines and Air India as statutory corporations.
2. Renaming of Imperial Bank as State Bank of India: On July 1, 1955, pursuant to the State Bank of India Act, 1955 and the recommendations of the All India Rural Credit Survey Committee, the Imperial Bank of India was nationalized and renamed the 'State Bank of India'.
3. First democratically elected communist party government in a state: In March-April 1957, following the general elections to the newly formed Kerala Legislative Assembly, the Communist Party of India (CPI) led by E.M.S. Namboodiripad formed the government in Kerala—the first democratically elected communist state government in the world.
4. Goa becomes part of independent India: In December 1961, the Indian Armed Forces launched 'Operation Vijay' to liberate Goa, Daman, and Diu from 451 years of Portuguese colonial rule, formally integrating it into the Indian Union via the 12th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1962.
Chronological Sequence: 3 (1953) -> 2 (1955) -> 1 (1957) -> 4 (1961).
Hence, the correct sequence is 3 - 2 - 1 - 4.
standard_book_ref: Bipan Chandra - India Since Independence; Ramachandra Guha - India After Gandhi
elimination_trap: Goa was liberated in 1961, making 4 definitely the last event in the sequence. This eliminates options A and D immediately. Comparing Air India (1953) with Kerala Communist government (1957) confirms 3 must precede 1.

mains_linkage.question: Discuss the political and constitutional significance of the formation and subsequent dismissal under Article 356 of the 1957 Communist ministry in Kerala.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Places Goa liberation (1961) before SBI renaming (1955) and Air India nationalization (1953).
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Inverts chronological progression.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Goa liberation happened in 1961, so 4 must be last.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: Accurate chronological order: Air India (1953) -> SBI (1955) -> Kerala CPI Govt (1957) -> Goa Liberation (1961), i.e., 3-2-1-4.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Precision post-independence chronological puzzle requiring specific decade-level event anchoring.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Places Kerala CPI govt (1957) before Air India nationalization (1953) and SBI (1955).
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Swaps political events with economic nationalization milestones.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Air India was nationalized in 1953, before Kerala 1957.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Places Goa liberation (1961) earlier in the sequence.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Chronology scramble.
option_analysis.mental_filter: 4 (Goa 1961) is the latest.

subject: Polity & Governance
sub_topic: Fundamental Rights - Right to Privacy (Article 21 & Puttaswamy Judgment)
question_text: Right to Privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of Right to Life and Personal Liberty. Which of the following in the Constitution of India correctly and appropriately imply the above statement?
options: Article 14 and the provisions under the 42nd Amendment to the Constitution
Article 17 and the Directive Principles of State Policy in Part IV
Article 21 and the freedoms guaranteed in Part III
Article 24 and the provisions under the 44th Amendment to the Constitution
explanation:
In the historic unanimous 9-judge Constitution Bench ruling in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (August 2017), the Supreme Court ruled that:
'The Right to Privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.'
The Court overruled previous judgments in M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962), holding that privacy is a natural, inalienable fundamental right that inheres in human dignity and personal autonomy, emanating from Article 21 and the broader cluster of liberties guaranteed in Part III (including Articles 14 and 19).
standard_book_ref: M. Laxmikanth - Indian Polity (Chapter: Fundamental Rights); Supreme Court Judgment in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. UOI (2017)
elimination_trap: A hallmark judgment of 2017; directly grounded in Article 21 (Right to Life and Personal Liberty) and Part III freedoms.

mains_linkage.question: Examine the three-fold proportionality test laid down in the Justice K.S. Puttaswamy judgment for state infringement of the Right to Privacy.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Article 14 guarantees equality before law; 42nd Amendment did not introduce the Right to Privacy.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Constitutional amendment distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Privacy is primarily anchored in Article 21, not 42nd Amendment.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Article 17 deals with the abolition of untouchability, unrelated to the privacy doctrine.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Article number distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Article 17 is abolition of untouchability.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: Verbatim phrasing of the Supreme Court's constitutional holding in the 2017 Puttaswamy privacy judgment.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Direct judicial doctrine test of a landmark constitutional verdict.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Right to Privacy = Article 21 and Part III freedoms.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Article 24 prohibits employment of children in factories and hazardous work.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Child labour article distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Article 24 is prohibition of child labour.

subject: Economy
sub_topic: Agricultural Economics - Minimum Support Price (MSP) Mandated Crops
question_text:
Consider the following :
• Areca nut
• Barley
• Coffee
• Finger millet
• Groundnut
• Sesamum
• Turmeric
The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs has announced the Minimum Support Price for which of the above?
explanation:
The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA), chaired by the Prime Minister, announces Minimum Support Prices (MSP) based on the recommendations of the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) for 22 mandated agricultural crops, plus a Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) for Sugarcane:
- 7 Cereals: Paddy, Wheat, Barley, Jowar, Bajra, Maize, and Ragi (Finger millet).
- 5 Pulses: Gram, Arhar/Tur, Moong, Urad, and Lentil (Masur).
- 8 Oilseeds: Groundnut, Rapeseed/Mustard, Toria, Soybean, Sunflower seed, Sesamum (Til), Safflower seed, and Nigerseed.
- Commercial crops: Raw cotton, Raw jute, and Copra (plus FRP for Sugarcane).
Analyzing the given crops:
1. Areca nut: Plantation crop, NOT covered under MSP.
2. Barley: Covered under MSP (mandated cereal).
3. Coffee: Plantation crop, NOT covered under MSP.
4. Finger millet (Ragi): Covered under MSP (mandated cereal/millet).
5. Groundnut: Covered under MSP (mandated oilseed).
6. Sesamum (Til): Covered under MSP (mandated oilseed).
7. Turmeric: Spice, NOT covered under MSP.
Therefore, the crops announced by CCEA are 2, 4, 5, and 6 only.
standard_book_ref: CACP Official Price Policy Reports; Ramesh Singh - Indian Economy (Chapter: Agriculture); Economic Survey
elimination_trap: Plantation crops (coffee, tea, areca nut/supari) and spices (turmeric, black pepper) are NEVER covered under CACP/CCEA MSP. Eliminating 1 (Areca nut), 3 (Coffee), and 7 (Turmeric) immediately eliminates options A, C, and D.

mains_linkage.question: Critically evaluate the pricing methodology of the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) for fixing Minimum Support Prices (MSP) in India.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Includes 1 (Areca nut), 3 (Coffee), and 7 (Turmeric), none of which are MSP-mandated crops.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Tests if candidate assumes all agricultural produce receives MSP support.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Plantation crops and spices have no MSP.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: Barley (2), Finger millet (4), Groundnut (5), and Sesamum (6) are all officially mandated MSP crops under the CACP framework.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Rigorous test of the 22 CACP-mandated crop list.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Eliminate Areca nut, Coffee, and Turmeric -> 2, 4, 5 and 6 only.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Includes 1 (Areca nut) and 3 (Coffee).
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Plantation crop trap.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Areca nut and coffee are excluded from MSP.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Includes all items including turmeric, coffee, and areca nut.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: All-inclusive trap.
option_analysis.mental_filter: CCEA does not announce MSP for spices or plantation crops.

subject: Environment & Ecology
sub_topic: Protected Areas - National Parks & Wildlife Sanctuaries of Northeast India
question_text: In which one of the following States is Pakhui Wildlife Sanctuary located?
explanation:
Pakhui Wildlife Sanctuary (also officially known as Pakke Wildlife Sanctuary and Tiger Reserve) is located in the East Kameng district of Arunachal Pradesh, nestled in the foothills of the Eastern Himalayas.
Declared a wildlife sanctuary in 1977 and a Tiger Reserve in 2002, Pakke is renowned for its conservation of four sympatric species of hornbills (Great Hornbill, Wreathed Hornbill, Oriental Pied Hornbill, and Rufous-necked Hornbill) and the pioneering community-based conservation partnership with the local Nyishi indigenous tribe (Hornbill Nest Adoption Programme).
standard_book_ref: PMFIAS - Protected Area Network: Arunachal Pradesh; Shankar IAS - Environment
elimination_trap: Direct protected area location recall. Pakke/Pakhui Tiger Reserve is famously situated in Arunachal Pradesh.

mains_linkage.question: Highlight the success of community-led conservation models in the Eastern Himalayas, citing the example of the Nyishi tribe and Pakke Tiger Reserve in Arunachal Pradesh.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: Pakhui (Pakke) Wildlife Sanctuary and Tiger Reserve is located in East Kameng district, Arunachal Pradesh.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Direct geographical recall of a premier Northeast protected area.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Pakhui / Pakke = Arunachal Pradesh (famous for Hornbill conservation).

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Manipur is home to Keibul Lamjao National Park (Loktak Lake) and Yangoupokpi Lokchao WLS.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Northeast state distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Pakhui is not in Manipur.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Meghalaya houses Nokrek National Park, Balpakram National Park, and Siju WLS.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Northeast state distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Pakhui is not in Meghalaya.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Nagaland hosts Intanki National Park and Fakim Wildlife Sanctuary.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Northeast state distractor.
option_analysis.mental_filter: Pakhui is not in Nagaland.

subject: Science & Technology
sub_topic: Space Technology - Launch Vehicles (PSLV vs GSLV Architecture)
question_text:
With reference to India’s satellite launch vehicles, consider the following statements :
• PSLVs launch the satellites useful for Earth resources monitoring whereas GSLVs are designed mainly to launch communication satellites.
• Satellites launched by PSLV appear to remain permanently ﬁxed in the same position in the sky, as viewed from a particular location on Earth.
• GSLV Mk III is a four-stage launch vehicle with the first and third stages using solid rocket motors, and the second and fourth stages using liquid rocket engines.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explanation:
Evaluating the statements regarding India's satellite launch vehicles:
1. Statement 1 is correct: The Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) was developed primarily to deliver Earth observation and remote sensing satellites into Sun-Synchronous Polar Orbits. The Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) was designed to launch much heavier INSAT/GSAT communication satellites into higher Geosynchronous Transfer Orbits (GTO).
2. Statement 2 is incorrect: Satellites launched by PSLV into polar or low-Earth orbits circle the Earth from pole to pole every 90 to 100 minutes; they do NOT remain permanently fixed in the same position in the sky. It is geostationary communication satellites (launched into equatorial orbits at ~35,786 km altitude by GSLV) that appear fixed relative to an observer on Earth.
3. Statement 3 is incorrect: GSLV Mk III (LVM3) is a three-stage launch vehicle: Stage 1 consists of two solid rocket boosters (S200); Stage 2 is a twin-engine liquid core stage (L110); and Stage 3 is an indigenous cryogenic upper stage (C25). It is PSLV that is a four-stage vehicle (solid-liquid-solid-liquid), not GSLV Mk III.
standard_book_ref: ISRO Official Portal - Launchers (PSLV & LVM3); Science Reporter
elimination_trap: Statement 2 falsely claims polar orbit satellites remain fixed in the sky (confusing Sun-synchronous polar orbit with geostationary orbit). Statement 3 claims GSLV Mk III is 4-staged, whereas GSLV Mk III is famous as a 3-stage vehicle.

mains_linkage.question: Compare the technological architecture, staging, and payload capabilities of ISRO's PSLV and LVM3 (GSLV Mk III) launch vehicles.

option_analysis.label: ✅ Official UPSC Key
option_analysis.diagnosis: Only statement 1 is correct: PSLV is designed for earth observation and GSLV for communication satellites. Statements 2 and 3 are factually flawed.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Precision rocket staging and orbital mechanics test.
option_analysis.mental_filter: PSLV orbits poles (not fixed); GSLV Mk III is 3-staged. Only 1 is true.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Statement 2 is scientifically false because polar orbit satellites move across the sky continuously.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Confuses Polar orbit with Geostationary orbit.
option_analysis.mental_filter: PSLV satellites do not appear fixed in the sky.

option_analysis.label: Trap
option_analysis.diagnosis: Statement 3 is false: GSLV Mk III has 3 stages (two solid boosters, liquid core, cryogenic upper stage), not 4 stages.
option_analysis.examiner_craft: Swaps PSLV's 4-stage configuration with GSLV Mk III's 3-stage configuration.
